#5508. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5506. Hardware-testing and engineering startup Nominal raises $240M at $3B valuation

Artificial intelligence-powered hardware-testing and engineering software startup Nominal Inc. today announced it has raised $240 million in new funding led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners.

The investment triples the company’s valuation to $3 billion, up from $1 billion cemented in March after it raised $80 million in a Series B-2 funding round. Additional major investors in the Series C round included Lux Capital, Sequoia, General Catalyst, Founders Fund, Avenir, Salesforce Ventures, M13 and Lockheed Martin Ventures.

Nominal assists engineers with hardware development by supporting testing and development. Engineers must piece together data from disconnected testing systems to understand how a machine performed under realistic conditions and understand what needs fixing.

The platform brings that information together, automates testing, and uses AI to help analyze the results. This shortens the cycle between testing and design, enabling faster improvements and iterations.

The challenge in the field isn’t collecting more data; there are plenty of ways to get that from simulation, sensors, video, and more. Hardware tests generate streams of sensor readings, logs, video and simulation results that all need to be analyzed together to create a whole picture of what happened. The company’s AI agent, Nominal Analyst, investigates that data and performs analysis based on the underlying evidence.

“Hardware engineering is getting its AI moment, with real operational value that goes far beyond making existing workflows faster,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Cameron McCord. “The companies building the world’s most advanced machines have decades of hard-won knowledge in their organizations.”

The company said it built its AI Intelligence Platform to bring together all the systems needed for testing and design assistance. It has multiple layers, including connections to engineering applications, the agent infrastructure, the data and finally the physical world through sensors.

Examples of what Nominal’s AI product works with alongside engineers include aircraft, rocket engines, autonomous vehicles, drones and energy systems. Engineering data and documentation associated with the hardware fed to the agents help during the development process to investigate performance, compare tests and check results against requirements.

The company said the challenge is putting engineers’ knowledge to work and connecting it to data so engineers can take on harder problems than wiring up tests. The objective is to let them sit down, smooth out challenges and address what looked impossible before.

“Engineers stay in command, with purpose-built AI helping them do their best work,” added McCord.

Nominal works with the tools engineers already bring, including application programming interfaces, Model Context Protocol and SQL for database queries. Developers can also directly access the platform to connect tools, build custom applications, and create their own workflows and agents.

The company said more than 80 commercial and government organizations use its platform, including five of the seven biggest defense contractors. Nominal’s customers include defense technology company Anduril Industries Inc., military shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls Industries Inc., known as HII, and high-speed aircraft developer Hermeus Corp.

#5505. Trump strikes a softer note on immigration; builders need proof

Trump said immigration policy may be too tough and suggested a deal for long-term undocumented workers. Administration signals remain mixed as ICE raids and arrest targets pressure builders ahead of 2027.  AI Summary

On Sunday, President Donald Trump indicated that he is open to negotiating an immigration deal with the incoming Democratic Congress. However, despite softening post-election rhetoric, the Trump administration appears to be sending mixed signals on immigration, clouding the outlook for any potential bipartisan agreement.

The stakes of the nation’s highly contentious immigration debate remain high for homebuilders. After a surge in job site raids by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) this summer and fall, many homebuilders say their workers, including those in the country legally, were swept up in enforcement actions.

Whether a bipartisan immigration deal materializes remains an open and pressing question for the numerous builders facing ongoing job site disruptions.

Speaking to CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Sunday, President Trump suggested his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough” and may have contributed to last week’s election outcome.

“When you go into a hotel…and you have a woman that’s worked there as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress – a lot of good things, great jobs – and all of a sudden, they’re being taken out of the country. It’s tough. It’s a tough thing,” Trump said.

Trump added that it may be “doable” to reach an agreement allowing undocumented workers who have lived in the U.S. for many years, construction workers among them, to legally remain in the country.

“Get the killers out. Get the rapists out. Get all the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out, but let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” Trump suggested.

It’s unclear whether Trump’s softer rhetoric will translate into a bipartisan immigration deal. However, his administration’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, a longtime immigration hardliner, to White House Chief of Staff suggests an agreement may be less likely than Trump implied in his CBS News interview.

And in a post on Sunday, the Official White House Rapid Response account, in a post on X, denied that Trump will push for an amnesty deal with Democrats.

However, Trump has at times shown a willingness to soften his stance on immigration, at least briefly. In June 2025, the Trump administration momentarily directed ICE to pause job site raids in sectors like agriculture, hospitality and restaurants after facing blowback from business leaders worried about staffing shortages.

Within days, however, the administration reversed course. It later set a target of 3,000 ICE arrests per day, leading to a record number of immigration arrests in recent months.

Trump has also helped kill a bipartisan deal before. In early 2024, ahead of the presidential election, he urged Republicans to vote against a Senate border package introduced by Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) that would have tightened asylum requirements, ended releases of migrants into U.S. communities while they await hearings, and let the president close the border when asylum claims surged. The bill ultimately failed.

Some homebuilding organizations, like the National Association of Home Builders, now have their eyes on a different bipartisan measure, the Dignity Act, which would allow certain undocumented workers to remain in the U.S. without citizenship. Trump’s words signaled openness to such a proposal, but the administration’s actions since the election suggest otherwise.

Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, laid out in a post-midterms election post on X that the administration may be open to changing its approach to immigration, with less room for negotiation.

“Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement – by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote.

For homebuilders, immigration policy and its impact on the construction labor pool remains among the biggest policy questions heading into 2027. However, history suggests that a bipartisan deal may be a heavy lift, as Washington hasn’t passed comprehensive immigration reform since 1986, under President Reagan.

Whether Washington breaks its four-decade drought on immigration reform, and whether enforcement eases on job sites, remains a key policy wild card to watch in 2027.

#5503. On theCUBE Pod: Blue wave sends AI stock plunging

The very blue results of last week’s midterms have sent technology investors into a tailspin.

With many successful candidates running on platforms opposing data centers and calling for greater restrictions on artificial intelligence, investors anticipate a slowdown in AI spending. Tech stocks fell, with a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap, and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5.5%.

“Yesterday was a bloodbath,” said John Furrier (pictured), executive analyst for theCUBE Research. “It was brutal here and the tech stocks got pounded. 41 states had data centers on the ballot. They all lost or won, depending how you look at it. Now it’s so mainstream, it’s a political football. So you’re starting to see the reality of AI. It’s hitting everybody. Everyone is impacted.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, right), chief analyst for theCUBE Research, discussed the fallout from the midterms and whether or not AI companies will really suffer in the long term. They also explored who will own the “system of intelligence” that will govern enterprise AI.

After the “bloodbath” last week, the question remains: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Despite the shockwaves from the midterms, theCUBE’s researchers are predicting a longer path toward monetization. A recent analysis identified 2029 as the highest-risk year for the AI bubble.

“There’s a clock in terms of the data center monetization and financing and how long it takes to build data centers,” Vellante said. “We know anybody who can sell GPUs is making money but the enterprises aren’t yet self-funding. I had said that by 2026, this year, you’re going to start to see clear evidence of monetization in the enterprise. I think you see it, but you’re seeing it within tech companies.”

Tech companies are applying AI more effectively, according to Vellante, which should not come as a surprise. He thinks the tech titans are in a solid position while neoclouds are taking on a greater share of risk by pioneering a new software model, although not all of them will make it in the long term.

A GPU-based AI economy will shift in the next several years, Furrier believes, which could lead to surprising winners and losers.

“Supermicro [Inc.], good numbers, [Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Arista Networks, Marvell Technology Inc.],” he noted. “My take is this: the infrastructure is evolving beyond GPU-centric computing. Networking, optics, memory, storage, power efficiency. System-level architecture is becoming the strategic advantage, and those bottlenecks are being solved by the companies I just mentioned. You saw the news that Marvell closed a $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum.”

The stock market plunge shows that not everyone is going to make it through the AI era’s eventual slowdown. Public opinion on data centers is mixed, to say the least, so companies will need to establish a foothold in the developing system of AI intelligence to remain competitive.

“Neoclouds like CoreWeave are going to make it through,” Vellante said. “They’re the first movers and they’ve got some quality advantages but they’re going to go through some pain. Hyperscalers are like an ATM. They could dial it down at any point in time … but right now it’s all about growth, it’s about footprint, it’s about market share.”

Who owns the “system of intelligence”? This layer, which will bridge the gap between intelligent agents and the data systems they depend on, appears to still be in play. Palantir Technologies Inc. has the ontology that could give it the edge, while Snowflake Inc. and Databricks Inc. are still developing the operational systems — though Vellante sees the latter as having one of the best strategies.

“You need determinism to own that system of intelligence,” Vellante said. “So I think it’s wide open. Right now, I think Ali Ghodsi [chief executive officer of Databricks] has the best vision. He’s going after the client surface, he’s going after the system of intelligence, he’s going after the governance catalog, he’s going after the agent action layer, and he’s partnering … with all the frontier model vendors. Whether or not they can pull it off, we’ll see.”

Frontier models are the “wild card,” as Vellante puts it, but at the moment, all the tech companies are trying to get a slice of the pie. Despite the recent market shakeups, Furrier sees AI-native enterprises as the ultimate result of this current period of growth.

“The AI-native enterprise or businesses is going to be the model,” Furrier said. “Everybody wins in that one. Compute providers, hyperscalers, the data platforms that are on the right side, and the application companies, which are basically going to be agentic. That’s going to be the winners on the profit concentration. The control point … it’s not going to be the models, it’s going to be data and context, and the agents will be the proof point.”

#5502. Century Communities names Jim Francescon as president

Century Communities Inc. announced that Jim Francescon, currently executive vice president of corporate operations, will be promoted to president effective Jan. 1, 2027. In his new position, Jim will oversee homebuilding operations, land and related corporate functions, building on his work leading recent acquisitions in Texas and Tennessee.   AI Summary

Century Communities Inc. (NYSE: CCS) announced on Monday that Jim Francescon has been promoted to president, effective Jan. 1, 2027, as part of the company’s long-term succession planning process.

The company, ranked 13th by sales volume in the HousingWire Homebuilder Rankings, said Dale Francescon will continue to serve as executive chairman. Rob Francescon, who currently serves as chief executive officer and president, will remain CEO.

As president, Jim Francescon will oversee Century Communities’ homebuilding operations, land and related corporate functions and will help drive the company’s strategy and growth, according to the announcement.

“Today’s announcement reflects the implementation of a succession plan that our Board, Rob, and I have been planning and executing over the past two years,” Dale Francescon, executive chairman of Century Communities, said in a statement. “We have been very thoughtful in how we have approached succession, with the goal of best positioning Century for long-term alignment with shareholders, success and growth.”

“Jim has played an integral role in shaping our strategic direction and our growth into one of the largest homebuilders in the country, including leading our recent acquisitions that have deepened our footprint and strengthened our platform,” Rob Francescon, CEO of Century Communities, said. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with Jim and our entire executive team as we position Century for continued success.”

Jim Francescon said he is “honored to take on this role and grateful to our Board, Dale and Rob for their confidence.”

“We have built a strong operating platform and a talented team, and I am excited about the opportunities ahead as we continue to grow and deliver on our promise of A Home for Every Dream®,” he said.

Francescon joined Century Communities in 2019 and most recently served as executive vice president, corporate operations, overseeing much of the company’s corporate operations, including homebuilding, land, strategy, business development, and mergers and acquisitions.

In that role, he led the company’s acquisition strategy, including recent acquisitions of HistoryMaker Homes, Anglia Homes and Landmark Homes of Tennessee, which expanded Century’s presence in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Nashville, respectively.

Before serving as executive vice president, Francescon was president of Century Living, the company’s multifamily platform, and earlier served as corporate vice president. Prior to joining Century, he worked in private equity at GoldPoint Partners, a subsidiary of New York Life Investments, and in investment banking at J.P. Morgan Securities LLC.

He holds a Bachelor of Science in business administration with a concentration in finance and real estate and a Master of Science in finance from the University of Denver. Francescon also serves as a trustee of the University of Denver, Children’s Hospital Colorado Foundation and ACE Scholarships Colorado.

Third Quarter 2026 Financial and Corporate Highlights

Selling, general and administrative, Research and Development

"During the third quarter, we continued strengthening Solidion Technology's financial foundation while positioning the Company for its next phase of growth," said Jaymes Winters, Chief Executive Officer of Solidion Technology. "We remain disciplined and opportunistic in our approach to acquisitions. Our healthy cash position and improved balance sheet provide us with the flexibility to continue to pursue opportunities that complement our existing technology and manufacturing capabilities."

"We believe our strategy positions Solidion Technology to capitalize on opportunities across the energy storage industry, while maintaining our commitment to long-term shareholder value."

For the remainder of 2026 and into 2027, Solidion Technology intends to remain an opportunistic and disciplined acquirer of revenue-generating assets and businesses in the battery storage sector that amplify its existing technology and IP portfolio while simultaneously advancing its commercialization initiatives and strengthening its manufacturing and commercial capabilities.

Solidion Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: STI) is an advanced battery technology company headquartered in Dallas, Texas, with R&D and manufacturing operations in Dayton, Ohio. Solidion develops silicon-rich anodes, solid-state batteries, and fire-retardant electrolytes designed to deliver higher energy density, improved safety, and lower cost for the electric vehicle, energy storage, consumer electronics, aerospace and defense, and AI data center markets, including next-generation backup power for data center operators. #5500. HECM endorsements rebound in October but stay near decade low

Federally insured reverse mortgage activity improved modestly in October 2026, with HECM endorsements rising 11% from September to 1,995, according to Reverse Market Insight and HECMWorld.com. The market remains near a 10-year low and slightly behind last year’s pace, with Finance of America, Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha dominating volume.   AI Summary

The federally insured reverse mortgage market posted a rebound in October, but activity remained at historically low levels compared to the past decade, according to data compiled by Reverse Market Insight (RMI) and published Friday by HECMWorld.com.

Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) endorsements rose to 1,995 in October, an 11% increase from September and the highest level in three months, the data shows. But even with the gain, this was the lowest figure for the month of October in at least 10 years.

Year to date, endorsements are about 3.19% below last year’s level — but comparisons are complicated by the federal government shutdown in October 2025, which disrupted activity and reporting.

Finance of America Reverse (FOA) remained the top HECM lender in October with 460 endorsements, followed by Longbridge Financial with 362 and Mutual of Omaha Mortgage with 332. Goodlife Home Loans posted 110 endorsements and Fairway Home Mortgage recorded 67.

Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha switched positions from September, and Goodlife jumped three spots by originating 62 more HECMs compared to the prior month. The top three lenders accounted for about 63% of all HECM endorsements in October, underscoring how concentrated the reverse mortgage business has become.

The number of active lenders with more than one HECM endorsement improved, rising to 75 in October from 63 in September.

From January through October, FOA widened its lead with 4,398 endorsements. Mutual of Omaha ranked second with 4,041, followed by Longbridge at 3,513, Goodlife at 916 and South River Mortgage at 692.

While endorsements increased, securitization volume moved in the opposite direction. HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) issuance in October was down 16% from September.

New View Advisors, citing its analysis of data from Ginnie Mae and private sources, reported that October HMBS issuance totaled $419 million, a decline of $27 million from September. There were 61 pools issued in October, nine fewer than in September.

FOA led all issuers in October with $180 million in HMBS issuance, up from $175 million in September. Longbridge and Mutual of Omaha saw month-over-month declines, issuing $116 million and $76 million, respectively.

First-participation pool production dropped to $238 million in October, down $28 million from September and $97 million from October 2025. New View said issuers “continue to struggle with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%.”

From January to October, FOA was the top first-participation HMBS issuer with $1.01 billion of issuance, according to New View. Longbridge followed at $863 million and Mutual of Omaha at $593 million.

In October, the 61 HMBS pools consisted of 14 first-participation pools and 47 tail pools. New View also highlighted the ongoing use of very small pools as 18 of the October pools had an aggregate size below $1 million, totaling $10.8 million of unpaid principal balance that might not otherwise have been issued.

#5499. ZEISS to expand myopia solutions in China with NMPA's approval of ZEISS PT LUNANA phakic intraocular lens

ZEISS Medical Technology showcased at CIIE its next-generation aspheric phakic intraocular lens (pIOL) PT LUNANAÂ® to address myopia in China, a growing major public health challenge for the region.

JENA, Germany, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ZEISS Medical Technology, one of the world's leading medical technology companies, announced its plans to extend ZEISS's established portfolio of solutions for addressing myopia with the recent approval from the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) in China for the PT LUNANAÂ® phakic IOL from ZEISS.

NMPA approval represents the company's first step in establishing the ZEISS phakic IOL portfolio. ZEISS PT LUNANA pIOL brings together ZEISS's cutting-edge optical technology and global ophthalmic workflow leadership with local expertise, R&D and manufacturing capabilities. ZEISS showcased its new pIOL at the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, China, with plans for its release in the coming year. ZEISS PT LUNANA pIOL features a next-generation aspheric optical design, AQUAFLEXÂ® hydrophilic polymer material and a broad selection of lens sizes and power options.

"As the impact of myopia continues to grow in China, advancing new solutions has never been more important. ZEISS PT LUNANA reflects our commitment to address this need through continued innovation, expanded treatment options and by enabling a more personalized approach to vision correction," says Andreas VÃ¶lker, Head of the Ophthalmology Strategic Business Unit, ZEISS Medical Technology. "The approval of ZEISS PT LUNANA represents more than a product milestone; it underscores our ambition to innovate in China and help shape a future where more people have access to advanced solutions for myopia."

"The strong momentum of the Chinese market is driving ZEISS's 'In China, for Global' innovation strategy," says Martin Fischer, President and CEO of ZEISS Greater China. "As we work with local partners to build an open and collaborative innovation ecosystem, ZEISS PT LUNANA exemplifies the success of this approach, combining breakthrough optical design with local agile responsiveness to support higher standards of vision health."

Myopia is a major public health challenge in China

China has an estimated 600 million people with myopia, with particularly strong demand for refractive surgery among young and middle-aged adults. As a growing number of young people enter adulthood with moderate-to-high myopia, the need for individualized refractive-care pathways will only grow. Recent research shows that two in three (67.2%) people aged 15 to 19 in China have myopia, with 9.5% having high myopia, according to a recent systematic review.1

The Work Plan for Accelerating the Provision of High-Quality and Efficient Eye Health Services (2026-2030) calls for increased coverage of effective refractive error correction. As one of the mainstream procedures for refractive correction, phakic IOL surgery has undergone more than three decades of clinical validation and gained widespread recognition among physicians and patients. However, as expectations increase for visual quality, demand for surgical options and interest in alternatives continue to rise, options for advanced phakic IOLs remain relatively limited. ZEISS PT LUNANA pIOLs were developed to address this gap, offering myopic patients in China a new, personalized option for refractive correction.

The ZEISS PT LUNANA pIOL is the first step in establishing a broader phakic IOL portfolio, driven by the company's rich optical heritage combined with local expertise and R&D. The first public showing at the CIIE marks the company's plans to expand its comprehensive refractive solutions, providing physicians with more vision correction options for a wider group of patients.

"Since the introduction of phakic IOLs, both physicians and patients have been looking forward to more diverse and innovative products and technologies. The debut of ZEISS PT LUNANA in China in the coming year will not only allow patients to benefit from this innovation firsthand but also will provide ophthalmologists with an opportunity to gain valuable clinical experience early on and strengthen their influence in cutting-edge academic research," said Professor Zhou Xingtao, President of the Eye and ENT Hospital of Fudan University, Shanghai.

ZEISS to extend refractive portfolio, expanding options for high-quality vision

ZEISS offers options for managing myopia throughout a person's lifetime, from MyocareÂ® lenses for children, Ortho-K lenses, and glasses through to refractive correction, such as SMILE proÂ® from ZEISS, and intraocular lenses. Patients seeking refractive correction options who are not suitable for laser correction may face challenges in finding a suitable solution for their individual eye conditions. ZEISS PT LUNANA integrates aspheric optical design into its next generation phakic IOL and features AQUAFLEX hydrophilic polymer material, designed for flexibility, clarity and stability. The phakic IOL will accommodate a wide range of myopia levels, as well as benefit and may provide a refractive correction option for patients with thin corneas or high myopia, who may not be candidates for laser vision correction.

Each patient's eyes are unique, making precise, individualized fitting essential for phakic IOLs. Professor Wang Xiaoying, Chief Physician at the Eye and ENT Hospital of Fudan University in Shanghai, emphasized that the ZEISS PT LUNANA pIOL offers a considered selection of seven lens sizes and 0.25-diopter increments, enabling physicians with greater choice when selecting a lens for individual patient needs. She added, "It supports physicians in their procedures and can help patients feel confident in their treatment choice."

Michael Achtelik, Global Head of Business Sector, Refractive Lasers, ZEISS Medical Technology, explained, "The NMPA approval in China marks an important step in our journey to bring the ZEISS phakic IOL portfolio to ophthalmic customers worldwide. By combining ZEISS' global expertise in precision optics and refractive workflows with local manufacturing expertise and market insights close to our customers in China, we are strengthening our ability to deliver more personalized solutions for patients across China."

ZEISS PT LUNANA has completed pre-market clinical trials and two years of follow-up at nine Grade 3A hospitals in China. ZEISS plans to commercialize this product in China first in 2027 and eventually will bring the platform to the global stage.

#5498. Cisco research: Trust, not technology, is now the speed limit on enterprise AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For several years, the conversation about enterprise artificial intelligence has focused on capability: which model is smartest and which GPU is fastest. That made sense when technology was the constraint.

It isn’t anymore. AI can now do far more than most organizations will allow, and the gap is trust.

That’s the core finding of “Permission to Scale: The Critical Role of Trust in Successful AI Adoption,” new research released today at Cisco Systems Inc.’s Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne. Authored by independent researcher Brad Howarth, the study draws on data from 25 Australian organizations.

At Cisco Live APJC, Cisco hosted a press panel to discuss the report. The panel, moderated by Howarth, featured a number of corporate leaders from companies that participated in the report, including Carl Solder, chief technology officer of Cisco ANZ (far left); Anna Tosky, chief people officer at Elmo Software (second from left); Chris Locke, CTO at Flight Center Travel Group (third from left); Naz Wilson, group culture and enablement manager at Funlab (third from right); and Lucio Ribeiro, chief AI officer at TBWA Australia (second from right).

Though a sample size of 25 is small, the results align with conversations I’ve had with corporate leadership. I appreciated the panel’s mix of technologies, human resources and cultural leadership. I also valued the mix of roles, as the biggest barrier to scaling AI isn’t technical but people-related.

Australia makes an interesting test case. According to University of Melbourne and KPMG research cited in the report, half of Australians use AI regularly, but only 36% trust it, and just 30% believe its benefits outweigh its risks. That’s the lowest among 47 countries surveyed. If you can build trust in AI in Australia, that work will scale globally. In the press release, Stefan Leitl, vice president and general manager of Cisco Australia and New Zealand, discussed the benefits of winning over this region: “It’s a playbook that travels well beyond Australia.”

Solder noted that among the six pillars in Cisco’s AI Readiness Index, chief information officers and CTOs gravitate toward what they know, namely infrastructure and data, and leave culture for others. He described a customer that invested in infrastructure, governance, data and information technology skills but “didn’t focus on the culture. And they found that there was a big pushback from their employees and customers on using the toolsets they’ve invested in.”

This is something I’ve seen repeatedly: Companies spend millions on AI platforms only to see utilization remain tepid. Howarth discussed an adoption “flywheel” in which successful use creates evidence, evidence builds trust and trust enables broader use. Companies sit around waiting for trust before deploying, and the evidence of trust must be something measurable.

Trust in AI needs to be established with realistic parameters. Many people reject AI after a single mistake, even though in most cases the error rate is much lower than that of people. This mirrors what the automotive industry went through when a Tesla accident would trigger a media storm. The reality is that Tesla’s Autopilot system experiences one crash for about every 7 million miles, compared with human drivers, who average about one crash every 1 million miles.

Perfection isn’t a realistic goal, but being faster and more accurate than others is. Users should understand this going into any kind of trial or proof of concept, as the expectation of perfection can erode trust.

Chris Locke offered a great example of an executive leading by example. The company’s 77-year-old founder, Graham “Skroo” Turner, uses AI every day. “He’s a big Anthropic Claude user,” Locke said. “This is also a guy who once said the internet wouldn’t catch on back in 2000. He may have gotten that one wrong, but he’s betting on AI catching on, so I think he gives us permission to play.”

Ribeiro outlined a more structured approach, describing trust as an equation built on four elements: ownership, competence, consistency and transparency. He was matter-of-fact about why asking a nervous workforce whether it wants AI doesn’t yield an accurate answer. “You never ask a barber if you need a haircut, as the answer is always yes.”

His alternative was honesty. Companies can’t promise to protect every job, but they can promise to make employees “the most prepared, trained, trusted person” if AI disrupts their role.

Funlab, where 79% of the workforce is 21 or younger, relies on peer learning. Its “AI Super Squad” convenes representatives from every department every four weeks. Wilson said early sessions simply clarified which tools were safe, because many employees’ real limitation was “just not knowing whether I am allowed to do certain things or not.”

The report’s central concept is calibrated trust. People need to know when to rely on AI, when to verify its outputs, and when a human must decide. Blindly trusting these systems and their outputs is a significant risk.

During the Q&A, I asked how companies protect against over-trust, especially in high-intensity jobs where people just take the answer and move on. Tosky was candid. “The AI slop. It’s real,” she said. “You ask the employee a question, prompt the AI system and then they send a report without looking at it, and it’s completely wrong. It’s 10 pages you now have to read.”

Elmo keeps a human in the loop on nearly everything, and she argued that the fix starts with redesigning the work. “It’s very unsexy, but start with the process itself, instead of just going, ‘OK, let’s throw a bunch of agents at it.'”

The report recommends that IT leaders adopt a specific practice: Stop treating log-ins as a proxy for trust, and track how often people challenge or override AI outputs. Usage shows people are clicking. Override rates show they’re thinking.

I also raised a contact center concern. AI automates the mundane tasks that served as cognitive breaks for agents, leaving them with nonstop, high-intensity work and higher churn. Tosky called it “AI brain fry” and suggested rethinking metrics and breaks. Wilson added that if AI absorbs routine work, employees lose the repetition that builds context and expertise. That’s a talent pipeline problem few companies are considering.

AI that drafts content is one thing; agents that act are another. Locke said Flight Centre now has agents handling a small subset of airline ticketing that was previously outsourced offshore, with security engaged from day one. He used AI to book his Uber to the event, but a return flight to Europe? “Not yet.”

Fewer than half of respondents are very or extremely confident that their foundations are ready for more autonomous AI, and more than half say their infrastructure needs upgrading. Cisco’s 2026 Relentless Defense report found that only 36% of Australian organizations apply consistent controls to AI agents and nonhuman identities. In the report, Lendi Group CTO Devesh Maheshwari described the target as “bounded autonomy, where the agent can act on your behalf but cannot go beyond the boundaries you have established.”

This is where Cisco can help its enterprise customers. Solder argues that trust must be enforced at the network and security layers. “Built into the network and security underneath, control stops being the brake and becomes the permission to move faster,” he said. Cisco is betting that its networking, security and Splunk portfolio will become the trust layer for agentic AI, and the report provides a business rationale for that bet.

As I stated above, the research is qualitative and aligns with what I hear from CIOs globally. My advice for IT leaders:

The AI winners won’t necessarily have the best models. They’ll have employees, boards and customers who trust the systems enough to let them do more. As Solder put it, “The leaders in our research aren’t scaling AI first. They’re scaling trust.”

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5497. Paraguay Bank Collapse Shows Why Bitcoin Was Created as USDT Hits Premium

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Paraguay bank crisis is showing why Bitcoin was created in the first place. USDT sellers reportedly demanded premiums of up to 13% after authorities placed major digital lender Ueno Bank into resolution.

MILLIONS of people LOCKED OUT of their own money as Ueno bank COLLAPSES IN Paraguay President Pena faces IMPEACHMENT — reports pic.twitter.com/3vb8z7MIQm

The crisis left 3 million customers temporarily unable to access their accounts. Some peer-to-peer (P2P) listings showed Tether’s USDT trading around 6,942 Paraguayan guaraníes. That compared with the central bank’s November 4 dollar reference of 6,144.02 guaraníes.

The USDT premium shows growing demand for dollar-denominated assets outside conventional banking. It also revives a question that shaped Bitcoin’s creation: what happens when people cannot freely access money held inside financial institutions?

The Central Bank of Paraguay initiated Ueno Bank’s resolution process on November 3. Regulators found its solvency ratio had fallen below half the legally required minimum following adjustments to its financial statements. Ueno itself had grown rapidly since launching in 2021, becoming one of Paraguay’s most prominent digital lenders.

The bank claimed 3 million customers and managed around $850 million in public funds. Following the intervention, the bank temporarily restricted customer access to accounts and disrupted financial services. Authorities began arranging account transfers and deposit protection while investigators examined the bank’s operations.

The crisis also triggered political fallout. President Santiago Peña announced his resignation on November 5 following mounting pressure over Ueno’s collapse. Reuters reported that prosecutors were investigating him, while authorities issued arrest warrants for eight bank executives.

Meanwhile, the USDT premium attracted attention across cryptocurrency markets. A November 5 review by Criptoinforme examined 80 Binance P2P advertisements. It found that the median price across the 10 best offers for buying USDT stood near 6,399 guaraníes. This represented a 3.4% premium over exchange-house dollar prices.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Paraguay’s banking problems carry an interesting historical connection to Bitcoin’s creation. Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin whitepaper on October 31, 2008, during the global financial crisis. It proposed a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that could transfer value without relying on financial institutions.

The message became even clearer when Nakamoto mined Bitcoin’s genesis block on January 3, 2009. Its embedded newspaper headline read: “Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.”

Bitcoin was designed to address the limitations of a financial system built around trusted intermediaries. Its decentralized network allows users to hold and transfer BTC without requiring permission from a conventional bank.

Paraguay’s situation demonstrates why that proposition still matters. If a bank restricts access to customer accounts, financial independence becomes more than an abstract crypto talking point.

Bitcoin takes another approach through decentralized ownership and self-custody. Users who control their private keys can access their BTC without depending on a bank to authorize withdrawals.

Bitcoin’s original promise was never simply about making investors wealthier. It was about giving people another way to hold and transfer value without depending entirely on the banking system. Paraguay has provided a timely reminder of why that idea emerged in the first place.

#5496. California voters reject measure to shred environmental red tape

California voters voted down Proposition 45, which sought to speed CEQA environmental reviews through standardized deadlines and faster court timelines. The measure lost 56% to 44% in unofficial returns, and the streamlining fight is expected to return to the Legislature.  AI Summary

California voters have rejected a ballot measure to speed environmental review of housing and other projects.

Proposition 45 would have consolidated a patchwork of legislative fixes to the California Environmental Quality Act, aimed largely at reducing a costly hurdle to building housing. The Associated Press called the race over the weekend, though the state is still counting votes. Unofficial returns showed about 56% of voters opposed and 44% in favor, a spread too large to overcome with the remaining votes.

It failed decisively across populous coastal counties, where housing affordability is a pressing concern. Voters in Santa Cruz, Marin and Sonoma counties rejected the measure by the widest margins.

Opponents tied the measure to data center development, an influential argument in midterm races nationwide.

“Californians have sent a clear message to corporate developers, utilities and data center builders that they will not stand for a broad assault at the ballot box on state law protecting our air, water and natural resources,” the Vote No on Prop 45 campaign released in a statement.

Proponents dubbed that an inaccurate scare tactic.

“The opposition relentlessly lied, falsely claiming that Prop 45 covered data centers when non-partisan experts agreed it did not – and used smokestack images and scare tactics about air and water pollution when the ‘essential projects’ included in Prop 45 did not include smokestack industries and also excluded mining, port, and other controversial projects,” Jennifer Hernandez, who leads Holland & Knight’s West Coast land-use and environmental group, told HousingWire TBD.

Opponents also countered the claim that the measure would help create affordable housing. They cited housing groups that urged a no vote or declined to endorse. Abundant Housing LA and California YIMBY, both of which endorsed L.A. Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, did not endorse the measure.

Opponents included the California Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters and the American Lung Association. Sierra Club California and the California Federation of Labor Unions also opposed it.

The California Chamber of Commerce sponsored the measure, with backing from home-builder groups and some affordable housing advocates.

“We were outspent but not outgunned, thanks to a broad bipartisan coalition that understood that Californians know we can have progress and safeguard our environment at the same time,” the campaign noted in its statement.

Had it passed, the measure would have capped full environmental impact reports at 365 business days. Court challenges would have faced a 270-day limit.

Covered “essential” projects included housing, water, energy, schools, health facilities and transportation. Applicants could have chosen the new procedures or the existing ones.

The Legislative Analyst’s Office said the measure could cost local governments up to $100 million a year at first. Long-term financial effects were unclear. A Chamber-commissioned analysis projected $1.5 billion in savings and added revenue over 10 years.

Prop. 45 followed a run of legislative changes that limited CEQA reviews of housing proposals. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131 in 2025. They exempted qualifying infill housing from CEQA and narrowed review for some projects falling short of an exemption.

A newer round of bills signed this fall targets more permitting delays. Some shield specific developments from further CEQA challenges. One is a major mixed-use development in San Diego.

Backers argued those fixes helped only some projects. They said project-specific exemptions left other developments exposed to years of delay. Prop. 45 would have applied common deadlines to all eligible projects.

Supporters said predictable timelines would help California build homes and the infrastructure that serves them. They said CEQA lawsuits add tens of millions of dollars in costs, and thwart efforts to increase housing supply by escalating entitlement risk. They also argued that the measure could cut delays by two to 10 years.

“Not-in-my-backyard” and environmental groups have long sued local governments under CEQA. Those suits typically argue agencies did not properly handle environmental impact reviews.

A study by Hernandez and other researchers reviewed 498 CEQA appellate decisions from 2013 through 2023. Agencies prevailed in 75%. But the study said prolonged litigation still stalls financing and raises costs. It covers appellate decisions only and predates the 2025 reforms.

Opponents said the 2025 reforms already addressed much of CEQA’s housing problem. They said Prop. 45 would cap public-comment periods, narrow tribal consultation and limit judicial review. They also argued that affordability was being used as cover for a developer advantage.

Critics said “essential” was defined so broadly that it could fast-track freeways, power plants and pipelines.

The fight to streamline CEQA may now shift back to the Legislature and a new governor.

“We know this fight is not over,” the No on Prop 45 campaign wrote in its statement.

“The good news is that many millions of Californians voted for Prop 45, and do want timely, accountable, and predictable outcomes in CEQA,” Hernandez said. “Our legislative supporters saw the dirty trick campaign tactics unfold, and now have the opportunity to adopt these important CEQA reforms for the ‘essential projects’ that California needs to restore affordability to our state.”

#5494. Alphabet’s Wing to invest $125M in new delivery drone factory

Wing Aviation LLC today announced plans to spend $125 million on the construction of a new delivery drone factory.

The initiative is part of a broader investment that also encompasses the Alphabet Inc. unit’s research and development teams in California. Additionally, Wing stated that it plans to invest in the communities where it operates. It currently offers deliveries in five U.S. cities and intends to bring its service to 14 more markets soon.

Wing is building its factory in Fort Worth, Texas. The 15,000-square-foot facility is expected to create up to 100 jobs. Wing says it will have capacity to make tens of thousands of delivery drones per year, which should significantly speed up its market expansion efforts.

The Alphabet unit’s drones reportedly have a wingspan of about 4.9 feet. They’re based on a frame made of styrofoam, a foam that mostly consists of trapped air, and carbon fibers. Styrofoam is lightweight and repels water, which comes handy when a drone is navigating challenging weather. The frame’s carbon fibers, in turn, boost its sturdiness.

The drone frame is equipped with 16 electric rotors that enable it to reach speeds of up to 60 miles per hour. Workers at stores that use Wing’s delivery service attach merchandise to its drones via a tether. After a drone takes off, it reels in the tether until the package comes into physical contact with its frame. When it reaches the customer’s house, the drone descends to an altitude of 20 feet and lowers the parcel.

Wing has built a software stack that automates much of the work involved in coordinating deliveries. It picks the most suitable drone for a given delivery run, plans its flight path and ensures that it won’t interfere with other drones. Human safety teams monitor for weather and air traffic changes that may make it necessary to adjust flight plans.

The unit plans to make its delivery service available to more than 40 million Americans by 2027. It’s pursuing the growth initiative in partnership with retailers such as Walmart Inc., which uses its drones to process e-commerce purchases. Last month, the latter company announced plans to make Wing deliveries available at more than 270 stores.

The Alphabet unit also intends to offer its service in Japan. Last month, it teamed up with Tokyo-based internet provider KDDI Corp. to make drone deliveries available to local consumers in 2027.

Although the drone delivery market is in an early stage, Wing already faces a significant amount of competition. In August, Amazon.com Inc. announced plans to make its Prime Air service available in nearly 500 U.S. markets by year’s end. More recently, drone delivery startup Zipline International Inc. raised $1.5 billion in funding at a $21.5 billion valuation.

#5493. LG Innotek Shines Again in Vehicle Lighting with Third Consecutive CES Innovation Award

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LG Innotek (CEO Moon Hyuksoo, 011070) announced on November 9 that its next-generation vehicle lighting module, Nexlide C+, has received a CES (Consumer Electronics Show) 2027 Innovation Award.

With its Nexlide series, LG Innotek has now received CES Innovation Awards for three consecutive years, from 2025 through 2027. The latest recognition reaffirms the company's world-class competitiveness in vehicle lighting technology.

Nexlide is LG Innotek's brand of next-generation flexible vehicle lighting modules, which combine the company's proprietary optical design with advanced materials technology. Built on surface light source technology, which emits light in a broad and uniform fashion, Nexlide modules are thinner and more compact than conventional vehicle lighting while allowing a wide range of design possibilities. LG Innotek holds more than 700 patents related to surface light source technology.

The key strength of the award-winning Nexlide C+ is that a single lighting module can produce two or more 3D images, known as the 3D Multi-Effect. For example, the same module displays a 3D image with a diagonal pattern when viewed from the left and a vertical pattern when viewed from the right. Because the image changes with the viewing angle, the lighting creates a dynamic visual effect with a sense of depth.

Nexlide C+ can be integrated into various parts of a vehicle, from exterior lighting such as taillights and front grille lights to interior ambient lighting.

An LG Innotek official said, "Vehicle lighting is evolving from a simple signaling function into a key factor that shapes the design competitiveness of an automaker's brand. Lighting technologies like Nexlide C+ that are capable of creating diverse light patterns will see even wider use."

Nexlide C+ is also ultra-slim, at just 3 mm (0.12 in) thick or less, allowing it to be installed in tight spaces within a vehicle. LG Innotek is the first in the world to apply Light Turning Film and 3D Micro-Optic Pattern Film to an ultra-slim surface light source module.

The Light Turning Film precisely controls the direction of light to make different images appear at different viewing angles, while the 3D Micro-Optic Pattern Film makes images look three-dimensional even on a flat lighting surface.

The two films are only about 0.16 mm (0.0063 in) and 0.13 mm (0.0051 in) thick, respectively. By incorporating these ultra-thin films into the lighting module, LG Innotek enables a variety of 3D lighting effects in a slim profile. Previously, achieving the same effects required optical components such as plastic lenses and reflectors, and installing multiple components made the lighting unit bulkier.

By using these films to reduce the thickness of the lighting module, Nexlide C+ gives automakers even greater design freedom.

Going forward, LG Innotek will actively promote Nexlide C+ to global automakers and parts suppliers, targeting a 2027 launch.

At CES 2027 in January, LG Innotek will showcase a broad lineup of next-generation vehicle lighting modules, including Nexlide C+, along with key components for various areas of physical AI, such as autonomous driving and robotics.

[Background] LG Innotek previously received a CES 2025 Innovation Award for Nexlide A+, the industry's first vehicle front lighting module to apply surface light source technology, with 40% less thickness and more than five times the brightness of the previous product. At CES 2026, the company received another Innovation Award for Nexlide Pixel, which reduced the lighting pixel size to among the smallest in the world while improving luminous efficiency by 30% compared with the previous product.

#5492. IBM builds on hybrid cloud and governance to advance its enterprise AI operating model

Enterprises are moving beyond AI pilots, putting greater emphasis on governance, production readiness and measurable business outcomes.

Research from Deloitte highlights a significant gap between enterprise AI ambition and execution: 54% of organizations plan to move at least 40% of their AI initiatives into production within six months. Yet only 25% have done so today. IBM is betting on its strengths — mainframe hardware, hybrid computing assets and a legacy of strong governance — to gain a leg up on the rest of the market, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante.

“In our opinion, IBM has found a differentiated path in enterprise AI by productizing workflow-level outcomes across a stack that, while sometimes confusing, customers generally trust,” he said. “Client Zero proof, a workload-first hybrid design, durable platforms reimagined for agents and a pragmatic quantum roadmap create a credible basis for sustained advantage.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of how enterprise AI has moved beyond the race for model supremacy, with major technology players now focused on enabling governed enterprise AI that delivers trust, reliability and predictable business outcomes. (* Disclosure below.)

IBM already has a substantial book of business around generative AI, with AI-related software sales and consulting engagements totaling more than $12.5 billion as of Q4 2025, up from $9.5 billion the previous quarter.

Through a series of investments, acquisitions and product launches, IBM is gathering assets for an enterprise AI operating model with four pillars: agent orchestration, trusted data, intelligent operations and governance.

Many of these capabilities were rolled out as part of a steady drumbeat of announcements leading up to IBM Think 2026 in May. In February, the company announced a partnership with Deepgram Inc. to integrate voice capabilities into watsonx Orchestrate, its enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing agents. Two months later, it made IBM Bob — an AI-assisted coding tool that helps developers plan, write, test, modernize and deploy code —  globally available.

In May 2026, IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent, the data streaming platform, to enhance watsonx.data. By integrating streaming and real-time data, IBM aims to make watsonx.data the trusted data foundation, providing AI agents with continuously updated context.

At Think 2026, the company repositioned Concert from a point product into an agentic IT operations platform designed to unify observability, optimization, security and automation across hybrid environments. The move positions Concert as the intelligent operations layer of IBM’s broader enterprise AI strategy.

The IBM Sovereign Core platform announced at Think 2026 is designed to address the final pillar: governance. It helps enterprises build and operate AI-ready sovereign environments by embedding governance, compliance and operational control directly into the underlying infrastructure.

June brought more AI-related announcements: IBM joined OpenAI’s Daybreak Cyber Partner Program, which aims to identify AI-driven cybersecurity threats. IBM has partnered with Google Cloud to help IBM consultants design, build and govern enterprise-grade agents on Google Cloud.

All these announcements paint a picture: IBM wants to be the one-stop shop for enterprise AI, and to do so, it is investing significantly in new capabilities while leaning on its reputation for trusted enterprise security and governance, according to theCUBE Research’s John Furrier.

“While others chase frontier models, IBM is betting on something harder: trusted AI in production,” he told theCUBE. “The question coming out of Think is simple — are they becoming the system of record for enterprise AI or just another layer in the stack?”

In a media briefing ahead of Think 2026, IBM Chief Executive Arvind Krishna pointed out that over 70% of all enterprise data remains locked up in on-premises systems. That makes hybrid cloud a critical component of IBM’s enterprise AI operating model, allowing enterprises to use corporate data for AI workloads without abandoning existing infrastructure.

Recent earnings reports appear to reinforce IBM’s bet on hybrid cloud in the AI era. Red Hat Inc., whose OpenShift Kubernetes platform underpins IBM’s hybrid cloud software portfolio, saw revenue increase 13% year over year. Meanwhile, revenue from IBM Z, the company’s mainframe platform, saw revenues grow 51% year over year, underscoring the continued importance of mainframes in IBM’s infrastructure business.

IBM is embedding AI technology directly into IBM Z mainframes to support demanding AI workloads, according to Ric Lewis, senior vice president of the Infrastructure Division at IBM.  This strategy has resonated with clients and led to 20%-30% program-to-program growth for almost a decade. Z mainframes, a key priority for enterprises looking to deploy AI while maintaining control over their data and systems, are also a pillar of IBM’s sovereignty strategy.

“Sovereignty is our home court. We do 70% of the world’s financial transactions,” Lewis told theCUBE. “The most important data that travels around the world is in our Z systems. Those are sovereign systems. They’re on-prem, they’re in environments, they’re in banks, they’re in financial institutions, they’re in insurance. Sovereign is our home court, and we know this space extremely well.”

IBM’s view of sovereignty centers on customer control: keeping critical data and AI workloads in environments customers own and govern, rather than depending entirely on third-party infrastructure. Javier Olaizola, global managing partner for hybrid cloud and data at IBM Consulting, explained that the topic is coming up earlier in client engagements.

“Sovereignty and exposure was coming in on slide 40 in a PowerPoint pitch,” he told theCUBE. “Now it’s coming up front: ‘How much is my exposure?’ That is coming up with a new set of conversations that we are having with clients.”

Sovereign Core is the company’s answer to those questions, according to Sripriya Srinivasan, general manager for Core and ALM software products at IBM. Its goal is to help companies maintain operational consistency even as AI regulations and geopolitics constantly shift. It also helps companies contend with massive AI agent sprawl.

“The proliferation of agents is real in enterprises. Everybody is starting to build agents,” Srinivasan told theCUBE. “How do you, as a [chief information officer], make sure that there’s a level of standardization, consistency, governance, orchestration? All of these are internal fears, not necessarily coming, just based on regulations.”

How does this all translate to real-world results? It’s useful to look back at Krishna’s comments from Think 2026, where he presented IBM’s point of view on what makes a successful enterprise AI strategy.

“The enterprises pulling ahead are not deploying more AI; they’re redesigning how their business operates,” Krishna said during a media briefing.

IBM sets its own example by viewing itself as Client Zero for its enterprise AI strategy, according to James Kavanaugh, senior vice president and chief financial officer of IBM.

“AI is now embedded across our business, from how we deliver services to our software portfolio to the capabilities we are adding to our infrastructure platforms and how we drive our own productivity,” he said.

IBM reports that more than 80,000 of its employees use IBM Bob, with users reporting more than a 45 percent increase in productivity. Additionally, IBM Consulting has deployed more than 4,000 digital workers across 450 active projects, including agents from watsonx, Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC.

To keep this digital workforce under control, the company relies on a management philosophy that treats AI agents like human workers, an idea that Krishna himself suggested, explained Mohamad Ali, senior vice president and head of IBM Consulting.

“Arvind called me, and we had a conversation about three years ago, and he said, ‘I want you to come over, and I want you to be a consulting business,’” he said in an interview with theCUBE. “‘What is digital labor? It’s a whole bunch of bits of software. I need you to come in, and I need you to build this set of software and do it in a way that it could be managed. You could think of this as HR management … but now you have to HR manage human workers and digital workers.’”

IBM customers are also putting elements of the enterprise AI operating model into practice. Global bank BNP Paribas SA has nearly 1,000 AI use cases underway across its operations, using a group-level framework with governance distributed across business units and functions.

“The strategy is to use AI, not to become AI — to use AI to better serve our customers and to give more value to them,” Jean-Michel Garcia, group chief technology officer at BNP Paribas, told theCUBE. “But also internally, for employees, to give them more capabilities to focus on the right set of tasks and to make them more efficient and more focused on what they do.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the IBM Think event. Neither IBM, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5491. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5489. Trump stands by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang despite spy scandal, but FBI is investigating

The revelations this weekend that Nvidia Corp. boss Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman who has been accused of working for Chinese intelligence have now ensnared U.S. President Donald Trump, raising further questions about national security.

At the same time, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said it’s looking into the affair, meaning it’s likely to get continuing attention in coming weeks or longer.

Nvidia said it has launched an investigation into Chief Executive Huang’s actions after he admitted to cheating on his wife with a woman known as Alice Huang (no relation), who serves as the CEO of a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.

U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang has been feeding information about Huang and the chipmaker’s plans to the Chinese government. And though Trump was informed of the possible infiltration, he has continued working with Nvidia and Huang on domestic policy issues related to technology and artificial intelligence, which have become of vital importance to the U.S. economy.

Huang has spent the last two years cultivating a close relationship with Trump, gaining extraordinary access to America’s top decision-maker and influence over the country’s AI strategy. He has gone from being virtually unknown to the president to being a key member of a cadre of technology industry executives accompanying him on trips aboard Air Force One, including a visit to China in May.

He has come to be seen as a major ally of Trump, attending numerous White House events while repeatedly praising his policies. Notably, his company made a $25 million donation to the president’s gaudy ballroom project, becoming its top corporate contributor alongside Apple Inc.

Those efforts seem to have gone a long way toward getting Huang into the president’s good graces, and it seems to have paid off for the company. Last year, after months of lobbying from Huang and Nvidia, the Trump administration agreed that it could sell more advanced chips to China that were previously banned from being exported to the country.

Though that decision was widely known, it seems that the Trump administration has intervened in other ways to protect Nvidia’s interests. Earlier today, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling banned chips into China, was abruptly canceled after receiving an email from Nvidia’s general counsel. Commerce official Jeff Kessler, who was nominated for the role by Trump, reportedly gave Nvidia permission to contact the investigation team and mention his name, which goes against standard protocol.

Investigators had grown suspicious that Megaspeed was essentially just a front for smuggling embargoed Nvidia chips into China, but the correspondence from Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter kicked off a kerfuffle that ultimately led to the investigation being transferred to the Department of Justice.

But Trump defended Huang late on Sunday, stating that the Nvidia boss is an “honorable guy” who has not committed any wrongdoing. The president had been briefed about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation as far back as October 2025, but decided not to do anything, according to the Times. “I haven’t heard that he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody, but, you know, so does everybody else.”

Trump continued to defend Huang on Monday when quizzed about the situation again, before revealing that the Federal Bureau of Investigation is also looking into his relationship with the suspected spy. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” he said at a White House briefing.

Despite the apparent protection afforded by Trump, Huang appears to be taking no chances. A report in Wired said today that the Nvidia boss has hired the services of a public relations firm called Heller that specializes in handling public scandals. Rise Heller, the firm’s founder, has developed a reputation for helping powerful men sidestep allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies. She previously represented clients including the former Congressman Anthony Weiner, the writer Jeffrey Toobin and the chef Mario Batali, Wired reported.

Tech industry personalities have also leapt to Huang’s defense. Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital said in a post on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” and stressed that although he did something “incredibly dumb,” he believes there was “no bad intention.” Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk later shared Maguire’s post, saying he agrees with all of it.

However, no intervention has managed to protect Nvidia’s stock, which slid more than 4% on Monday, wiping around $190 billion off of the company’s valuation.

Nvidia is scheduled to hold its next financial earnings call on Nov. 17, in which Huang is likely to face some very difficult questions — if he is on the call as has been customary.
