#5469. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5468. A CEO gave his employees Fridays off. Three years later, revenue is up about 160%

In late 2022, Jake Kurtz, founder and CEO of Tampa-based social media agency Brick Media, wanted a better work-life balance. He had a wild idea: What if everyone worked just four days a week?

After seeing European companies experiment with shorter workweeks on social media, he launched a 90-day pilot in January 2023, giving employees Fridays off without cutting their salaries. By April, he had made the schedule permanent.

Nearly four years later, Brick’s revenue has grown dramatically. According to figures the company provided, revenue jumped 73% in 2023, another 39% in 2024, and 8% in 2025. Compounded, that’s roughly 160% growth in three years.

Kurtz believes some of that success traces back to the four-day workweek, though he doesn’t claim the schedule alone explains it. He bets that giving employees a reason to stay makes the company more efficient and more competitive, even as workplace researchers say the four-day week has faded from the hybrid-work conversation and some leaders who tried it have dialed it back.

At Brick, employees work four nine-hour days, Monday through Thursday. That’s a 36-hour week, four hours short of the traditional 40, with paid lunch breaks included. Employees are still considered full-time and eligible for benefits.

That puts Brick between a compressed 40-hour week and the 32-hour model some researchers advocate. At Fortune’s Workplace Innovation Summit in May, University of Georgia psychology professor Malissa Clark argued that the point of a four-day week is to cut eight hours, not cram 40 hours into four days.

Brick’s schedule also contrasts with the long hours common in the related public relations field. Muck Rack’s State of PR 2026 report found that 55% of PR professionals surveyed had worked more than 40 hours the previous week.

Social media doesn’t exactly take weekends off, but Kurtz said clients have been surprisingly understanding of the arrangement, and most content shoots, meetings, and other work can be planned ahead of time.

Employees still occasionally handle small tasks on Fridays or weekends, which he described as taking “five minutes here and there.” He estimated that more serious emergencies requiring several hours of work happen roughly once or twice a quarter. In those cases, nonexempt employees are eligible for overtime if they work more than 40 hours in a week, and the company brings in freelance contractors when needed.

The rule he goes by: Don’t bury employees in work.

Brick served 56 clients in all of 2022, compared with 85 in just the first half of 2026, according to Kurtz. A social media manager typically handles six or seven clients, with seven the upper limit.

Once employees approach that threshold, Brick hires more people instead of piling more work on existing staff. That’s one reason revenue has grown so quickly. It’s also why profit margins have stayed roughly unchanged since 2022, Kurtz said, as payroll has risen alongside revenue.

Employees also work from home most of the time. Only one of the four working days requires a trip to the office.

For Kurtz, keeping employees happy is as much a business strategy as a cultural one.

“If I can keep people here longer, and they like their job, and they’re communicating with similar people all the time, it just makes the business a lot more efficient,” he told Fortune.

Experienced employees don’t need everything spelled out. Kurtz said colleagues who have worked together for years can sometimes resolve something in a two-minute hallway conversation that might otherwise take 30 minutes.

He believes that efficiency translates into better client relationships and, ultimately, more business. Of the 20 new leads Brick received in October, 16 came from referrals, according to Kurtz.

The company’s resignation numbers suggest employees are increasingly willing to stay. Brick recorded six voluntary departures in 2022, before the schedule change, compared with two in 2023, two in 2024, three in 2025, and none so far in 2026, according to figures provided to Fortune. Its workforce has grown from 15 employees at the end of 2022 to 25 today.

Asked whether Brick could have achieved the same success with employees on-site five days a week and working frequent overtime, Kurtz said, “No, I really don’t…I think people would leave Brick Media for like a $5,000 raise.” He said he knows some employees have had better offers and chose to stay.

“People have a hard time leaving the four-day schedule once they experience it, because they start to realize that life is way more than just the salary,” he said.

It’s the same case ThredUp CEO James Reinhart made on Clark’s panel at the Fortune summit, where he warned that companies sticking with five-day weeks will lose the competition for top talent.

For Andrea Echeverry, Brick’s director of client experience, who has been with the company since before the schedule change, switching to four days hasn’t meant doing less work.

“I think we have just found more ways to be more efficient with our time,” she told Fortune.

She doesn’t mind squeezing the same workload into four longer days. In fact, she prefers it. Echeverry said that “hustle culture has played a role,” explaining that people her age are still willing to work long hours but take a different approach to the traditional “work hard, play hard” mentality.

She is a working mother whose husband also works full-time, and Fridays are now for spending time with her child and running personal errands.

To Echeverry, it’s part of a generational shift in attitudes toward work. Rather than accept traditional workplace arrangements simply because previous generations did, she believes younger workers are more willing to question the norm.

She isn’t alone in ranking balance over pay. In Randstad’s global Workmonitor 2026 survey, 46% of workers named work-life balance as their main reason for staying in their job, compared with 23% who cited competitive pay and benefits.

“We’re sort of like redefining work-life balance,” she said.

Kurtz doesn’t think every company needs to give employees Fridays off. Instead, he advises other CEOs to “think about what would make your employees want to work at your company.”

“I just think that there’s a happy middle ground where you can still have a really good life and a really good business,” he said. “And if you can also extend that to your employees, then it’s not only a feel-good thing for the culture; it’s actually a business advantage that your competitors won’t have.”

#5467. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5466. AI Is Changing the Economics of SaaS Partnerships. Here’s How Founders Can Capitalize.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is reshaping the SaaS partner model, creating opportunities beyond traditional referral commissions and low-margin services.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A typical SaaS referral deal gives a partner 10-15% of first-year revenue, rarely enough to support sales, implementation and future growth. As SaaS made software easier to buy and deploy, much of the surrounding work became repeatable, pushing partners toward lower-margin services. Without a more profitable business to build around the platform, they will invest elsewhere.

AI gives partners something SaaS gradually took away: high-value work built on the platform, shaped by the customer’s context and sold as expertise rather than access. Not every AI engagement will be unique, nor should it be. The reusable parts like connectors, retrieval patterns, evaluation frameworks and managed operations will become more standard. But the decisions that make an AI system useful do not travel so easily from one customer to another. Which workflow should change? Which data can be used? Where does human review belong? What counts as a good answer, and who is accountable when it is wrong?

The building blocks may be familiar, but making the workflow safe, useful and adopted is not. It relies on industry judgment that the partner has built from years of being the person the client calls when something breaks.

This is not an argument that every partner should go train a model, or that every SaaS company should suddenly become a services business. Most customer deployments will be about workflow design, permitted data, integration, evaluation, governance and adoption, not fine-tuning a foundation model. The point is simpler: AI creates a new layer of work above the subscription, and the partners best placed to capture it are the ones who know the customer’s business well enough to make that layer valuable.

Futurum Research’s 2H 2026 partner survey found that 71% of active partners named custom application development as a primary growth driver, even as sentiment toward packaged enterprise software weakened. But that does not mean every bespoke build will be profitable. It does suggest that customers are looking beyond generic software for tailored engineering and that partners see more room in services than in a shrinking resale margin.

For SaaS founders, that changes the question from “How do we get partners to refer more deals?” to “What can partners build profitably with us?” Start by running the full math: referral and renewal income, plus the gross profit from partner-delivered implementation and AI services, minus the cost of acquiring and serving the account. If a partner can create a healthy contribution margin while making the product more useful to the customer, the program has a foundation. If it cannot, a higher referral percentage is just a more expensive version of the same problem.

The program should then make that work easier to do well. Give capable partners a sandbox that resembles production, not just a demo login. Train them on integration, evaluation, governance and escalation — not only on product features. Certify them against real use cases. Bring the strongest partners into the harder solutions early, before the vendor has decided every implementation detail in-house. That is how a platform becomes a place where partners can build expertise instead of merely resell a discount.

Measure the result accordingly. Referred ARR still matters, but it is only part of the picture. Track services revenue and margin where they can be observed, time to production, active use, product adoption, support burden, retention and the customer outcome the solution was designed to improve. Outcome-based incentives can work, too, if they are tied to milestones the partner can actually influence: a verified deployment, adoption by an agreed user group, a successful evaluation or a retained account after a defined period.

None of this removes the need for discipline. A vendor still needs clear data rights, guardrails, support boundaries and a view of who is accountable when a workflow fails. Partners need room to earn services revenue without creating a maintenance burden the vendor cannot support. Those are not reasons to stay with the old model. They are the operating details that turn the AI thesis into a business model.

The point is not that AI work will never commoditize. Some of it will, and it should. The point is that AI gives partners a larger, more defensible role while the work still depends on customer data, workflow knowledge and practical judgment. A program built around that role is harder to reduce to a commission table. It gives partners more reason to invest, gives customers more value from the platform, and gives the vendor something more durable than a better percentage to compete on.

A typical SaaS referral deal gives a partner 10-15% of first-year revenue, rarely enough to support sales, implementation and future growth. As SaaS made software easier to buy and deploy, much of the surrounding work became repeatable, pushing partners toward lower-margin services. Without a more profitable business to build around the platform, they will invest elsewhere.

AI gives partners something SaaS gradually took away: high-value work built on the platform, shaped by the customer’s context and sold as expertise rather than access. Not every AI engagement will be unique, nor should it be. The reusable parts like connectors, retrieval patterns, evaluation frameworks and managed operations will become more standard. But the decisions that make an AI system useful do not travel so easily from one customer to another. Which workflow should change? Which data can be used? Where does human review belong? What counts as a good answer, and who is accountable when it is wrong?

#5465. Lucid missed earnings expectations — and tapped its Saudi backer for $1.75 billion more

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Lucid's total liquidity would reach $3.75 billion with the expanded Public Investment Fund facility, up from $2.0 billion at quarter-end

Lucid $LCID Group fell short of Wall Street's third-quarter estimates on Monday, according to CNBC. The electric vehicle maker also announced a $1.75 billion increase to the size of a term loan facility it can tap in stages, provided by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, its anchor shareholder.

Lucid reported revenue of $350 million, up 4% from a year earlier, and a loss of $2.74 per share. Analysts compiled by LSEG expected revenue of $407 million and a loss of $2.28 per share, according to CNBC.

The net loss was $830.9 million, compared with $978.4 million a year earlier. The adjusted EBITDA loss was $726.3 million, compared with $717.7 million in the third quarter of 2025. Free cash flow consumption fell 30% from the prior quarter to $1.04 billion.

Lucid ended the quarter with $2.0 billion in total liquidity. With the increased facility, that figure would be $3.75 billion. The company said it expects that level to bankroll its day-to-day activity and major spending through Q4 2027, a window that covers the launch of production for its midsize vehicle.

"We are grateful for the continued financial support from our anchor shareholder, which further energizes us to remain focused on execution and on our commitments as we build a stronger, sustainable Lucid," CEO Silvio Napoli said in a statement, according to CNBC.

Lucid said it has achieved $0.8 billion in savings so far this year under its $1.4 billion cash flow improvement plan and remains on track to meet the full-year target. Construction of its second manufacturing plant in Saudi Arabia is progressing to plan, with inauguration expected in early 2027. Midsize production remains planned for the second half of 2027, and the company expects to announce reveal and production dates in the first quarter of 2027.

Lucid plans to share its medium-term roadmap and objectives in the opening months of next year. The company withdrew its forward outlook and several of its goals in May, according to CNBC, explaining that new management needed time to put together a turnaround plan.

The results follow the "operating reset" Napoli put in place after taking over as CEO in June. In early October, Lucid produced 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806 in the third quarter as it cut output to work down inventory. Its Arizona plant ran on a single shift for the full quarter after previously running two.

Lucid stock dropped about 5% in extended trading on Monday.

#5464. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is likely to keep his job for now, say prediction markets

Traders are already betting on whether embattled Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, will stay on as head of Nvidia. Platforms including Kalshi and Polymarket were quick to offer wagers on Huang’s future since the CEO acknowledged his affair Sunday, and the early results are in his favor.

One event contract on Kalshi asking when Huang will leave as Nvidia’s CEO has drawn more than $266,000 in trading volume. Traders put the probability of his departure before January 2029 at 54%, compared with 52% before January 2028 and 33% before July 2027. A separate Kalshi market has drawn roughly $2,500 in trading volume, with traders putting the probability that Huang will testify before Congress by next January at 46%, rising to 79% by next July.

Polymarket has also listed a market on when Huang’s resignation or removal as CEO will be announced, drawing more than $305,000 in trading volume. Traders put the probability of an announcement by year-end at 16%, rising to 22% by the end of March 2027.

Meanwhile, Polymarket is also offering wagers about Huang’s personal life. There are currently around $159,000 of bets on the probability of a divorce by March 2027, with current odds at 23%.

The event contracts come a day after Nvidia announced an investigation into Huang, who acknowledged to the company’s board that he had an intimate relationship with a business executive whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares have fallen nearly 10% since Monday morning.

With Huang’s future uncertain, traders have turned the corporate scandal into a running forecast of what could happen next, much as they do with other unfolding news.

These platforms allow users to trade on outcomes across sports, politics, and even the weather, with prices reflecting traders’ expectations of how events will unfold. They drew substantial attention during last week’s midterm elections, when traders favored Democrats to win control of both chambers of Congress.

The midterm results bolstered prediction markets’ reputation as forecasting tools. The platforms rose to prominence during the 2024 presidential election, when traders favored Donald Trump to win while polls showed a close race between him and Democratic candidate Kamala Harris.

But the platforms’ forecasts have not always matched the results. While prediction markets broadly anticipated Democratic gains in the midterms, they favored Republicans in the Texas governor’s race and South Carolina’s Senate race, both of which Democrats ultimately won.

An earlier surprise in Brazil’s presidential election also raised questions about the platforms’ forecasting accuracy.

#5463. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.

#5462. Skydance is planning at least $6 billion in cost cuts after Warner Bros. deal

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The company expects the savings within three years as it combines Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery operations

Skydance laid out a plan to cut at least $6 billion in costs within three years after closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The company described the plan in a letter to shareholders on Monday, which accompanied a Form 8-K filing.

The company said new leadership teams are in place and integration work is under way. It expects the savings to come from merging duplicate streaming platforms, studio units, television networks and corporate departments, all within a cost structure that exceeds $50 billion, according to CNBC.

Skydance projects savings of $2.2 billion or more from trimming administrative and corporate overhead, such as layers of management, heavier reliance on artificial intelligence and a smaller office footprint. Streamlined marketing and promotional spending would account for at least $1 billion, and unifying streaming and broadcast technology for about $1.4 billion. A further $1.4 billion would come from consolidating third-party spending and purchasing under one group.

Skydance pointed to the Paramount $PARA cost program as a model. That program is expected to produce more than $2.7 billion in annualized efficiency gains before 2026 ends, Skydance said.

Some reductions have started. Skydance began offering voluntary buyouts last month ahead of layoffs and adopted a five-day in-office policy. Eight executives, four from Warner Bros. and four from Paramount, left last week.

Skydance reported third-quarter results for Paramount Skydance, covering the period before the Warner Bros. Discovery deal closed. Revenue rose 5% to $7.03 billion, and net income was $73 million, compared with a loss of $257 million a year earlier. The company said it will give full-year guidance when it reports fourth-quarter results.

Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6, and the company said then that it was targeting at least $6 billion in run-rate synergies within three years. The combined company trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker "SKYD."

The letter repeats a medium-term outlook for 2030 of mid-single-digit annualized revenue growth, mid-20% adjusted EBITDA margins and more than $10 billion in free cash flow. Skydance also plans to offer a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle early next year, as a step toward combining the two services.

#5461. Before news broke of his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Nvidia’s Huang told Fortune his company “could be of great service” to China

Jensen Huang’s dealings with China and views on U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips are under fresh scrutiny after the Nvidia CEO confessed to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly believe to be working as a spy for China. The U.S. has spent years restricting the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China on national security grounds.

In an interview Fortune conducted before the allegations surfaced, Huang said that he thought the chipmaker “could be of great service” to China. He also said that Nvidia had a “large and growing” opportunity in China.

Huang spoke to Fortune in mid-October, before The New York Times first reported later that month that U.S. officials had concluded the woman, Alice Huang—who has no relation to the Nvidia CEO—was a Chinese intelligence asset. It isn’t clear how long the relationship lasted, but photos shared online show the two together in Taipei as early as June 2024.

Asked in October whether he expected sales in China to pick up, Huang said there would be a “natural tension” between Washington and Beijing that “lasts a long time,” adding that Nvidia would continue to give shareholders no guidance on its China sales. The company has left China out of its revenue forecasts since August 2025, citing regulatory uncertainty in both countries.The U.S. has not allowed Nvidia to sell its most advanced AI chips to China, but has granted the company export licenses for older models of its graphics processing units (GPUs), the specialized chips that run AI and computer graphics applications. It has allowed Nvidia to market specialized versions of its GPUs in China that have been designed specifically for that market and which are engineered to be less capable at training frontier AI models. Beijing, for its part, has officially tried to bar the country’s major tech companies from buying Nvidia’s chips as part of an effort to spur demand for domestic alternatives.

Nonetheless, Huang told Fortune he saw promise in the Chinese market. “I think the opportunity in China is large and growing, just like the AI market across the world is large and growing,” Huang said. “We could be of great service to the local market. We can compete and win as much of the AI market as possible for the United States, while also providing compute resources, which is really important to their economy.”

China has been a long-running headache for Nvidia. Back in 2022, the Biden administration imposed export controls that barred Nvidia from selling its most advanced AI chips to China, aiming to slow Beijing’s progress in AI and its potential military applications. Nvidia designed scaled-down chips for the Chinese market, but successive rule changes cut many of those off too.

Since then, Huang has continually pushed for more access to the Chinese market. In October 2025, after export controls and Beijing’s pushback had shut Nvidia out of the market, he complained that the company had gone from 95% market share in China to 0%.

In December 2025, President Trump reversed course on some of the Biden-era restrictions, allowing Nvidia to ship its H200 chips—which are designed to comply with U.S. export controls—to approved Chinese customers, with the U.S. government taking a 25% cut. The decision came after months of lobbying by Huang, who met with Trump to discuss export controls days before the announcement. Nvidia’s complicated history with China has been dragged back into the spotlight by Huang’s confession to the extra-marital affair. In Sunday’s memo to staff reviewed by Fortune, he admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, after the Financial Times reported on a U.S. government memo describing a romantic relationship between him and Alice Huang. “There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote in the memo. “I am deeply sorry.”

The same day, Nvidia’s board announced that a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, would examine whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. The board said it so far had “no reason to believe” either had been. For now, Huang remains CEO and said he would cooperate fully with the review.

U.S. officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was working for China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center operator where she was an executive, has become one of Nvidia’s largest customers over the past two years. Its Malaysian affiliate bought at least $4.8 billion in equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to the Times. U.S. officials have scrutinized the company since 2024 over suspicions it helped Chinese firms evade export controls.It is suspected that, despite U.S. export controls, the leading Chinese AI companies have access to large computing clusters of Nvidia’s advanced GPUs, obtained either through large-scale smuggling operations, or through data centers in other Asian nations that they have accessed using front companies.

Nvidia has previously told news outlets that Huang’s dealings with Alice Huang were routine, and a company spokesperson told Fortune: “Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.”

Megaspeed also did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment, and Alice Huang could not be reached. China’s foreign ministry called the allegations “pure groundless speculation and slander.”

The Republican chairs of three House committees have asked Huang to attend a private briefing the day after Nvidia reports quarterly earnings next week. Lawmakers are likely to press Huang on whether his push into China has put U.S. interests at risk.

In October, he told Fortune that Nvidia could put American customers first and still compete abroad.

“The United States recognizes that because the technology is invented in the United States, and we’re an American company, we should provide, and we do provide, the best, the soonest and the most to American companies. However, we should compete,” Huang told Fortune during the interview. “AI is a five-layer cake, and America should go compete at every single layer, not just the model layer.”

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. #5460. Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 5, 2026 at 2:27 pm

Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning, the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org, the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.

“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM, which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.

Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who took an interest in climate modeling before his death in 2018. His company, then known as Vulcan, launched the climate modeling project in 2019, and the group moved to Ai2 in 2021. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.

In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.

Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.

Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect date for the start of the climate modeling effort at Vulcan. It started in 2019.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5459. You Don’t Need a Full-Time Executive to Get C-Suite Expertise. Here’s Why.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

For entrepreneurs, there are lots of good reasons to hire on a fractional basis — but it might not be right for everyone. Here’s my take.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Hiring full-time workers is a commitment, especially at the C-suite level. As a solopreneur myself, it took me a long time before I had the resources to bring anyone on to help shoulder the responsibilities of running my business.

But a lot has changed since I launched my company back in 2006. Now, fractional executives—leaders who share their expertise with organizations on a part-time basis—are quickly becoming the norm. In fact, research has found that the number of workers describing themselves as “fractional” has tripled since 2018; among executives, the most common limited roles are CFOs, followed by CMOs.

For entrepreneurs, there are lots of good reasons to hire on a fractional basis. The right fractional executive can bring valuable expertise, fresh perspective and strategic guidance without requiring the long-term investment of a full-time hire. But it might not be right for everyone. Here’s my take.

Several factors have conspired to create the recent boom in fractional work. Post-Covid-19, more people are seeking out flexible roles and the ability to work multiple part-time jobs. At the same time, a tough job market has produced a surplus of highly skilled workers, while many companies don’t have the funds to fill those roles full-time.

Leadership roles are also simply growing more complex. Between the proliferation of hybrid work and AI adoption, it stands to reason that expertise is also becoming more varied. In general, high level roles are changing, with AI automating several functions previously handled by executives, like operations and reporting. On the other hand, demand for a la carte, specialized skills are on the rise — maybe your organization needs someone fluent in transitioning to an AI-powered workforce, but only on a limited-time basis.

You’d be forgiven for thinking fractional executives are just consultants by another, buzzier name. But the truth is they’re quite different.

The main distinction is that, while they do work on a part-time basis, fractional executives are embedded in your team. They make decisions that drive outcomes and are responsible for what happens as a result.

Consultants, on the other hand, operate outside the organization. They make recommendations, but are not ultimately accountable for how things turn out. For example, a consultant can analyze your pricing strategy and show you a presentation on how they think it can be improved. A fractional CFO, on the other hand, will rebuild the pricing model themselves, and answer for the numbers at the quarter’s end.

Before you hire someone touting themselves as a fractional executive, dig into the details of what they’re offering and make sure they — and you — understand the difference.

Fractional work may be a product of our current moment, but it’s also unlikely to go away any time soon.

For entrepreneurs, the perks of such roles are many. Benefits packages, equity and long-term salary commitments are not part of the equation. You get the expertise without the long-term overhead, and you can scale the relationship up or down as your needs change.

But fractional isn’t free of tradeoffs, and it isn’t right for every role. Start by asking a few questions:

It’s entirely possible that a fractional hire can turn into a full-time offer once the time is right. But understanding the role, its limitations and whether it’s the appropriate fit for your business is key. A fractional hire doesn’t need to feel like a compromise, because it shouldn’t be. Handled correctly, it’s a deliberate way to get the right expertise at the right time, without pretending your company needs something it doesn’t.

Hiring full-time workers is a commitment, especially at the C-suite level. As a solopreneur myself, it took me a long time before I had the resources to bring anyone on to help shoulder the responsibilities of running my business.

But a lot has changed since I launched my company back in 2006. Now, fractional executives—leaders who share their expertise with organizations on a part-time basis—are quickly becoming the norm. In fact, research has found that the number of workers describing themselves as “fractional” has tripled since 2018; among executives, the most common limited roles are CFOs, followed by CMOs.

For entrepreneurs, there are lots of good reasons to hire on a fractional basis. The right fractional executive can bring valuable expertise, fresh perspective and strategic guidance without requiring the long-term investment of a full-time hire. But it might not be right for everyone. Here’s my take.
