#5457. 15 GLP-1 side effects, from most to least likely, including rare vision loss

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These GLP-1 side effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide, from common nausea to rare vision loss linked to semaglutide, are ordered from most to least likely

One of the ways GLP-1 drugs work is also behind many of their most common downsides. Semaglutide, sold as Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus, and tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, slow the rate at which the stomach empties. Food lingers longer, people feel full sooner, and they tend to eat less. That same slowdown helps explain why the digestive tract registers most of the complaints.

These medicines imitate glucagon-like peptide-1, a hormone the gut releases after eating. Tirzepatide also acts on a second gut hormone, known as GIP. Both drugs were first approved to treat type 2 diabetes. Wegovy and Zepbound are the versions approved for chronic weight management.

The 15 GLP-1 side effects below are a selection, not every reaction these drugs can cause. They are ordered from most to least likely, based on the broad pattern in clinical trials of semaglutide and tirzepatide. Exact frequencies differ by drug and dose. They also differ between people treated for type 2 diabetes and people treated for obesity. For that reason, the order reflects tiers of likelihood rather than precise percentages.

Digestive effects sit at the top. Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation are the most frequently reported, followed by abdominal pain. Many of these peak in the first weeks of treatment or right after a dose increase. Prescribers raise doses in steps to give the body time to adjust.

The middle of the list covers effects reported less often, such as headache, fatigue and dizziness. It also includes indigestion, gas and bloating, reactions where an injection is given, and hair thinning linked to rapid weight loss.

The final stretch covers less common but more serious problems that appear as warnings on the drug labels. Gallstones, gallbladder inflammation and pancreatitis belong in this group. Each one has warning signs that call for prompt medical care.

Vision loss comes last because it is the rarest item here. The condition, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, causes sudden vision loss through reduced blood flow to the optic nerve. In June 2025, the European Medicines Agency's safety committee classed it as a very rare side effect of semaglutide. That conclusion concerned semaglutide specifically. Any sudden change in vision still needs urgent medical attention.

Nausea is the side effect people report most often on GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide. It is usually worst in the first weeks of treatment and after each dose increase, then tends to fade as the body adjusts.

The queasiness has a physical basis. GLP-1 medications delay the movement of food out of the stomach and into the small intestine. A meal sits in the stomach for longer than usual. That can leave it feeling heavy or unsettled, particularly after a large or rich meal.

The drugs also act on the brain. GLP-1 receptors are found in brainstem regions involved in appetite and nausea. Activity there is thought to help curb hunger. It may also contribute to the sick feeling some patients describe.

For most people, the nausea is mild to moderate and temporary. The prescribing information for the semaglutide and tirzepatide brands describes digestive reactions in those terms. Even so, gastrointestinal effects were the most common reason trial participants stopped taking these drugs.

Gradual dose escalation is the main tool doctors use to keep nausea manageable. Each brand's label sets out a schedule that begins well below the maintenance dose. The amount rises in fixed steps, with a gap of weeks between increases. The same approach applies to Rybelsus, the tablet form of semaglutide. The Ozempic label states that its starting dose is meant to begin treatment and is not effective for blood sugar control. Its role is to give the digestive system time to adapt.

If a step is hard to tolerate, a prescriber can hold a patient at the current dose for longer. The Wegovy label allows dose escalation to be delayed when a dose is not tolerated. Doctors can also decide not to move a patient up to the highest available dose.

Eating habits matter too. Common clinical advice includes eating smaller meals, eating slowly and stopping at the first sign of fullness. Fried, greasy and very fatty foods are frequent triggers. Fat slows digestion on its own. Combined with the drug's effect, it can leave a meal sitting even longer.

Nausea that worsens instead of easing deserves a call to a doctor. The same applies when it comes with repeated vomiting. Persistent symptoms can signal dehydration or another problem that needs medical attention.

Diarrhea ranks among the most frequent digestive side effects of GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide. It is usually mild to moderate. It tends to cluster around dose escalation, the weeks when a patient moves up to a higher dose.

Each new dose level gives the gut something fresh to adjust to. Loose stools that faded at one dose can return for a short spell after the next increase. The effect is reported with the weekly injections and with Rybelsus, the oral semaglutide tablet.

In most cases the problem eases as treatment continues. Episodes that persist or worsen are a different matter. They are worth reporting to the prescriber rather than waiting out.

The main concern with severe diarrhea is dehydration. Repeated watery stools carry water out of the body, along with electrolytes such as sodium and potassium. Plain water replaces the fluid but not those salts. An oral rehydration solution replaces both.

Significant fluid loss reduces blood flow to the kidneys. The prescribing information for semaglutide and tirzepatide warns of acute kidney injury in patients who become dehydrated from severe gastrointestinal reactions. Some of those cases have required hemodialysis.

The risk weighs most heavily on people who already have reduced kidney function. The labeling advises monitoring kidney function in patients with kidney impairment who report severe digestive reactions.

Early signs of fluid loss include darker urine, urinating less often, a dry mouth and unusual thirst. These signs indicate that fluid intake is not keeping pace with what the gut is losing.

Over-the-counter antidiarrheal medicines are widely sold. A prescriber or pharmacist can advise whether one is appropriate alongside a GLP-1 drug and other medications a patient takes.

Prescribers have options when diarrhea does not ease. They may keep a patient at the current dose for longer before the next increase. They may also step back to a lower dose. The dosing schedules in the labels allow for that flexibility, and the decision rests with the clinician.

Vomiting is one of the more common digestive side effects of GLP-1 drugs, though it is reported less often than nausea. It usually arrives alongside nausea. The bigger concern is often not the episode itself but the fluid the body fails to hold onto afterward.

Clinical trials of semaglutide, sold as Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, place vomiting among the most frequently reported reactions. Rybelsus, the oral semaglutide tablet, carries a similar digestive profile.

Episodes tend to cluster in the first weeks of treatment and in the days after a dose increase. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are both raised in steps, typically every four weeks, until a patient reaches a maintenance dose.

Persistent vomiting creates a specific dehydration problem. A person who cannot keep water down loses fluid faster than they can replace it, even when they keep trying to drink. Repeated vomiting also drains electrolytes such as potassium and sodium. The body relies on those minerals for normal muscle and heart function.

That fluid loss can reach the kidneys. The prescribing information for semaglutide and tirzepatide warns that acute kidney injury has been reported in patients who became dehydrated from nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. Some of those reports involved people with no known kidney disease.

Several signs suggest vomiting has moved beyond a nuisance. They include being unable to keep any liquids down, passing very little or very dark urine, and a persistently dry mouth. Those symptoms call for prompt contact with a clinician. A prescriber may delay the next dose increase, lower the dose or pause the medication.

Vomiting paired with severe abdominal pain that spreads to the back is a different situation. That combination can signal pancreatitis, and it needs urgent medical care.

Day-to-day management usually centers on eating habits. Common advice includes smaller meals, stopping at the first sense of fullness and cutting back on fatty or fried foods. Fatty meals leave the stomach more slowly. Small sips of clear fluids between episodes are easier to tolerate than large drinks taken at once.

In clinical trials, digestive reactions such as vomiting were the most common reason participants stopped treatment because of side effects. For most people who continue, episodes become less frequent once they settle on a steady maintenance dose.

Constipation is one of the most frequently reported digestive effects of GLP-1 drugs, alongside nausea, diarrhea and vomiting. It is listed as a common adverse reaction in the prescribing information for semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

The link runs through the gut's pace. These medicines slow how quickly food leaves the stomach, and they also slow movement further along the digestive tract. When stool moves more slowly through the colon, the body draws more water out of it. The result is harder, drier stool that is more difficult to pass.

Eating less adds to the problem. GLP-1 drugs reduce appetite. Many people respond by eating smaller meals. Smaller meals usually mean less fiber and less overall bulk reaching the bowel. Some people also drink less when they feel full, which leaves less fluid to soften stool.

Constipation is generally defined as having fewer than three bowel movements a week. Other signs include straining, hard or lumpy stools and a feeling that the bowel has not fully emptied. A clear change from a person's usual pattern can also be a sign. On a GLP-1 drug, constipation can occur alongside bloating or mild cramping.

Standard management advice focuses on fluid and fiber. Drinking water through the day helps keep stool soft. Fiber-rich foods such as vegetables, beans, whole grains and fruit add bulk. Fiber tends to work best when fluid intake rises with it. Adding fiber gradually can limit extra gas. Regular physical activity, including walking, also supports normal bowel movement.

Over-the-counter options exist, including osmotic laxatives and stool softeners. Anyone considering them should check with a prescriber or pharmacist first, especially if they take other medicines.

Constipation is usually manageable, but some symptoms need prompt attention. Severe or worsening abdominal pain, a swollen belly, vomiting or an inability to pass gas or stool can signal an intestinal blockage. Ileus is a condition in which the intestines stop moving their contents along. The U.S. prescribing information for Ozempic lists ileus among reactions reported after the drug reached the market.

Abdominal pain is one of the more frequently reported GLP-1 side effects, and most episodes are mild and pass on their own. Severe pain that does not ease, especially pain that spreads to the back, is different. It calls for prompt medical attention.

The prescribing information for semaglutide, sold as Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus, lists abdominal pain among its common adverse reactions. The labels for tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, list it as well.

The everyday version tends to feel like cramping, aching or a sense of pressure in the stomach area. It is most likely in the first weeks of treatment or soon after a dose increase. For many patients, it fades once the body settles into the new dose.

Meal size plays a role. These drugs keep food in the stomach longer. A large or high-fat meal can sit heavily as a result. Eating smaller portions and stopping at the first sign of fullness is standard guidance for managing digestive discomfort on these medications.

Noting when the pain starts can also help. A simple record of dose days, dose changes and symptoms gives a prescriber a clearer picture. It can show whether the pain follows a pattern or is getting worse over time.

The warning signs look different from routine discomfort. Pain that is severe, constant or sharp deserves attention. So does pain that moves from the abdomen into the back, or that comes with repeated vomiting. Fever, or yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes, is another reason to seek care.

Those symptoms can point to pancreatitis or gallbladder disease. Both are labeled warnings for GLP-1 drugs. Both are far less common than ordinary stomach upset. The semaglutide medication guides tell patients to stop the drug and call a health care provider right away if severe stomach pain will not go away.

The practical line is persistence and severity. Mild cramping that comes and goes after a dose change is a known pattern. Intense pain that lingers, spreads or arrives with other symptoms is a reason to stop and get checked rather than wait it out.

Headache is a reported side effect of GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide. It shows up less often than nausea, diarrhea and the other digestive complaints that dominate reports from people taking these medications.

Why GLP-1 medications are linked to headaches has not been firmly established. Several features of treatment could play a part, but none has been confirmed as the cause. A person with frequent headaches on these drugs may need to rule out more than one possible trigger.

Eating less is one possible contributor. These drugs reduce appetite, and many people end up skipping meals or eating much smaller portions than before. Going long stretches without food is a familiar headache trigger for some people, whether or not they take any medication.

Fluid intake is another candidate. People who feel full or queasy often drink less along with eating less. Mild dehydration is a common cause of headache in general. It can build gradually when drinking feels unappealing.

Blood sugar is a separate consideration for people with type 2 diabetes. GLP-1 drugs on their own carry a low risk of pushing blood sugar too low. That risk rises when they are combined with insulin or with sulfonylureas such as glipizide. Low blood sugar can bring on a headache along with shakiness, sweating, confusion and a racing heartbeat. A headache that arrives with those symptoms calls for a glucose check.

General headache-care habits apply here. Eating small, regular meals instead of skipping them can help. So can sipping water through the day. Keeping a note of when headaches occur relative to each dose can help a prescriber spot a pattern.

Anyone considering an over-the-counter pain reliever should check with a pharmacist or prescriber first. That matters most for people who take other medications or have kidney problems. Drugs such as ibuprofen can strain the kidneys.

Some headaches need prompt medical care regardless of the drug. A sudden, severe headache that peaks within about a minute is an emergency. So is a headache with a stiff neck, fever, weakness on one side of the body, slurred speech or confusion. Those signs should not be put down to a routine side effect or waited out.

A headache that keeps returning, or that worsens after each dose increase, is worth raising with the prescriber. Slowing the escalation schedule or staying at the current dose for longer are options a doctor can weigh.

Fatigue is a commonly reported side effect in clinical trials of semaglutide and tirzepatide. People describe it as tiredness or low energy, and no single cause has been established for it.

Fatigue has been reported in trials of these drugs for both type 2 diabetes and weight management. It is reported less often than the main digestive complaints.

Lower calorie intake is one possible contributor. Reduced appetite on these drugs often means eating far less than before treatment. A body running on fewer calories can feel sluggish. That connection has not been confirmed, and it is not the only possible explanation.

Other side effects can overlap with tiredness. Nausea, vomiting or diarrhea can disrupt sleep. They can also make it harder to eat and drink normally. A person dealing with those symptoms may feel drained even if the drug is not the direct cause of the fatigue.

Diet quality becomes more important when appetite drops. Smaller meals leave less room for protein, fruit, vegetables and whole grains. A doctor or registered dietitian can help plan meals that still cover basic nutritional needs on a reduced intake.

Blood sugar is a separate issue for people with type 2 diabetes. The prescribing information for semaglutide and tirzepatide warns that the risk of low blood sugar rises when they are combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Tiredness paired with shakiness, sweating, confusion or a fast heartbeat can signal low blood sugar. A glucose meter reading can confirm it.

Fatigue that does not lift, or that gets worse over time, should be raised with a doctor. Tiredness has many causes unrelated to medication, including anemia, thyroid problems, poor sleep and depression. Blood tests can help rule some of these out.

If side effects make daily life difficult, doctors can slow the pace of dose increases. That adjustment can apply to tiredness as well as to digestive symptoms.

Indigestion, known clinically as dyspepsia, is a recognized upper-digestive side effect of semaglutide. The prescribing labels for Ozempic and Wegovy both list it among the drug's common adverse reactions.

Dyspepsia describes discomfort centered in the upper abdomen, just below the breastbone. People often report a burning sensation, a heavy or overly full feeling after eating, or fullness after only a few bites. It differs from nausea, which is the urge to vomit. It also differs from cramping lower in the abdomen.

Ozempic and Wegovy share the same active ingredient, and Novo Nordisk makes both. Wegovy, the weight-management version, goes to a higher maximum dose than Ozempic. Indigestion appears on the side effect lists for both drugs. That means it can affect people treated for type 2 diabetes as well as people treated for obesity.

The issue is not unique to semaglutide. The labels for tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, also list dyspepsia as a common reaction.

Indigestion on these medications can overlap with acid reflux. Gastroesophageal reflux disease, in which stomach acid backs up into the esophagus, also appears among the gastrointestinal reactions in the semaglutide labels. Heartburn behind the breastbone, a sour taste or regurgitation point toward reflux rather than simple indigestion.

Meal habits are the usual first step in managing it. Smaller portions, slower eating and stopping at the first sign of fullness reduce the load on the stomach. Fried, greasy and very rich foods tend to aggravate symptoms. Staying upright for a while after meals and avoiding late-night eating can limit reflux.

Persistent indigestion should be raised with the prescriber. A prescriber may adjust the dosing schedule or check for other causes. Chest pain that spreads to the arm, jaw or back should not be assumed to be indigestion. The same goes for chest discomfort that comes with shortness of breath. Those symptoms need emergency care because they can signal a heart problem.

Dizziness is a less frequent GLP-1 side effect than the digestive complaints, but it appears at a modest rate in trials of semaglutide and tirzepatide. It usually feels like lightheadedness, often on standing up, rather than a spinning sensation.

No single mechanism has been established. Two possible contributors stand out. One is a shortfall of fluid in the body. The other is a drop in blood pressure that can accompany weight loss.

Fluid intake often falls on these drugs. People who feel full sooner tend to eat and drink less. A meaningful share of daily water normally comes from food. A body running low on fluid has less blood volume in circulation. That can leave the brain briefly short of blood flow when a person stands.

Blood pressure is the second possible contributor. Weight loss tends to lower blood pressure, and GLP-1 drugs have been associated with modest reductions in clinical trials. For someone already taking blood pressure medication, the combined effect may push readings lower than intended. Doctors sometimes reduce or stop those medications as weight comes down.

Blood sugar can matter for people with type 2 diabetes. A GLP-1 drug used on its own carries a low risk of hypoglycemia. The risk rises when it is combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea such as glipizide. Lightheadedness, shakiness and sweating can signal a low reading. A glucose meter can confirm it.

A few practical steps address the likely triggers. Rising slowly from a bed or chair gives circulation time to adjust. Drinking fluids steadily through the day helps when appetite is low. Home blood pressure checks can show whether a medication change needs discussing with a prescriber.

Some dizziness is not routine. Fainting, a racing or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, confusion or dizziness that does not let up warrants prompt medical attention. Older adults face a higher risk of falls. Even mild unsteadiness in an older person is worth raising with the prescribing doctor.

Bloating, belching and gas are common digestive side effects of GLP-1 drugs. The prescribing information for semaglutide products such as Ozempic and Wegovy lists abdominal distension, eructation and flatulence among their common adverse reactions.

Those three clinical terms describe familiar complaints. Abdominal distension is the swollen, tight feeling of an overfull belly. Eructation is the medical word for belching. Flatulence is gas passed from the lower bowel.

The three complaints often appear together. GLP-1 drugs slow the rate at which the stomach empties into the small intestine. A meal that stays in the stomach longer can leave a person feeling full and stretched for hours after eating.

Belching usually comes from swallowed air. Eating quickly adds air to the stomach. So do carbonated drinks, chewing gum and drinking through a straw. Some people on these medications describe belches with a rotten-egg smell, often called sulfur burps. That odor comes from hydrogen sulfide, a gas produced when sulfur-containing compounds break down in the gut.

Lower-bowel gas has a different source. Bacteria in the colon ferment carbohydrates that the small intestine does not fully absorb. That fermentation releases gas. Beans, lentils, onions, broccoli and cabbage are common contributors. Sugar alcohols such as sorbitol, found in many sugar-free sweets and gums, can have the same effect.

Practical steps focus on how and what a person eats. Smaller meals put less volume into a stomach that is already emptying slowly. Eating slowly and stopping at the first sign of fullness can limit both pressure and swallowed air. Clinicians commonly advise people on these drugs to cut back on fizzy drinks and on fried or very fatty meals. A short food log can help pinpoint which meals trigger the worst episodes.

Like most digestive effects of this drug class, gas and bloating are usually mild. They tend to be more noticeable early in treatment or after a dose increase.

Ordinary bloating is different from a belly that becomes hard, swollen and painful. Severe pain, repeated vomiting or being unable to pass gas or stool needs prompt medical care. Those signs can point to a bowel blockage. The semaglutide labels list ileus, a condition in which the intestine stops moving its contents along normally, among reactions reported after approval.

Injection-site reactions are a generally minor GLP-1 side effect that shows up as redness, itching or swelling where the dose goes in. They affect the injectable forms of these drugs, not the oral semaglutide tablet sold as Rybelsus.

Most GLP-1 medications are given as a shot under the skin. Ozempic and Wegovy, both semaglutide, are injected once a week. So are Mounjaro and Zepbound, the tirzepatide brands. Older drugs in the class, such as liraglutide, sold as Victoza and Saxenda, are injected once a day. A daily schedule means more needle sticks over the same period.

The shot goes into the fatty layer under the skin rather than into muscle. The prescribing instructions name three areas for it: the abdomen, the thigh and the upper arm. A reaction typically stays small and local. It can look like a pink patch, a raised bump, mild tenderness or a minor bruise around the puncture point.

Rotating the injection site is the main step the drug labels describe. The instructions tell patients to change the spot with each dose. That can mean switching between body areas. It can also mean moving to a different spot within the same area.

People who also take insulin get a specific instruction. The Ozempic label says the two drugs should be given as separate injections and never mixed. They may go into the same body region, but the injections should not sit right next to each other.

Rybelsus is a daily tablet approved for type 2 diabetes. Its label carries separate instructions to take it on an empty stomach with a small amount of water.

A local skin reaction is different from an allergic reaction to the drug. Serious hypersensitivity is a labeled warning for GLP-1 medications. Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat calls for emergency care. So do trouble breathing, a very fast heartbeat or a widespread rash. Redness that keeps spreading, feels hot or produces pus after an injection also needs a doctor's attention. Those changes can signal an infection rather than a routine reaction.

Hair thinning is a recognized side effect of GLP-1 treatment and appears in the label for Wegovy, Novo Nordisk's semaglutide drug for weight management. It is generally linked to the speed of weight loss rather than to a direct effect of the drug on hair follicles.

The pattern resembles telogen effluvium, a common form of temporary hair shedding. At any moment, most hairs on the scalp are in a growth phase. A physical shock to the body can push a larger share of follicles into a resting phase at the same time. Those hairs then fall out together weeks later.

Rapid weight loss is one of the known triggers. Others include major surgery, childbirth, high fever and severe illness. People who lose large amounts of weight after bariatric surgery often report the same kind of shedding. That overlap suggests the weight loss itself is the shared factor.

The delay can make the connection hard to spot. Shedding from telogen effluvium typically shows up two to three months after the trigger. A person may notice more hair in the shower or on a brush well after the first weeks on semaglutide or tirzepatide.

The thinning is usually spread across the whole scalp rather than concentrated in patches. Hair often looks less dense, particularly along the part. The condition does not scar the follicles. In most cases, shedding slows and regrowth begins within several months once the trigger settles.

Diet can play a part. GLP-1 drugs reduce appetite, and eating much less can lower intake of protein, iron and other nutrients that hair needs to grow. Low iron and low protein intake are both associated with hair shedding. A doctor can order blood tests to check iron stores, thyroid function and other possible causes.

Patchy bald spots, scalp redness or shedding that continues for many months point to something other than weight-loss shedding. Those signs call for a separate medical evaluation. Any decision to change a dose or stop treatment belongs with the prescribing doctor.

Gallstones and gallbladder inflammation, known as cholecystitis, are labeled warnings for GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide. They occur less often than the digestive complaints that dominate trial reports. When they do occur, they can require hospital care or surgery.

The gallbladder is a small, pear-shaped organ that sits beneath the liver. It stores bile, a digestive fluid the liver makes to help break down fats. After a meal, the gallbladder contracts and pushes bile into the small intestine.

Gallstones form when substances in bile harden into solid deposits. Most are made largely of cholesterol. They can be as small as a grain of sand or as large as a golf ball. Many people carry gallstones without symptoms and never learn they are there.

Rapid weight loss is a known risk factor for gallstones. When the body sheds weight quickly, the liver releases extra cholesterol into bile. The gallbladder may also empty less often, which lets bile sit and thicken. The same pattern is well documented after bariatric surgery, another source of fast weight loss. Weight loss on GLP-1 drugs may raise gallstone risk through this route. Whether the drugs also act on the gallbladder directly is less settled.

Baseline risk also varies from person to person. Women develop gallstones more often than men, and the risk rises with age.

Cholecystitis usually develops when a gallstone blocks the duct that drains the gallbladder. Bile backs up, and the organ becomes inflamed. Without treatment, the inflammation can lead to infection. In severe cases, the gallbladder wall can tear.

The prescribing information for these drugs tells patients to watch for specific symptoms. They include upper abdominal pain, fever, clay-colored stools and yellowing of the skin or eyes. Gallbladder pain often centers on the upper right side of the abdomen. It can spread to the right shoulder or the back and may last for several hours.

Doctors typically confirm gallstones with an abdominal ultrasound. For people with repeated attacks or cholecystitis, the usual treatment is surgical removal of the gallbladder, called a cholecystectomy. Most of these operations are done laparoscopically through small incisions. People can still digest food without a gallbladder. Bile then flows directly from the liver into the small intestine.

Pancreatitis, an inflammation of the pancreas, is an uncommon but serious labeled warning for GLP-1 drugs. Its main warning sign is severe, persistent abdominal pain that may spread to the back, with or without vomiting.

The pancreas sits behind the stomach. It makes digestive enzymes that break down food. It also makes hormones such as insulin that help control blood sugar. In pancreatitis, those enzymes become active inside the organ and irritate its own tissue. The result is swelling and pain, and in severe cases lasting damage to the pancreas.

The prescribing information for semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) carries a pancreatitis warning. The labels tell clinicians to watch for signs of the condition. They also say to stop the drug if pancreatitis is suspected.

Whether GLP-1 drugs directly cause pancreatitis is still under study. The warning reflects cases reported in people taking these medications. It is not proof that the drug triggered each case.

Pancreatitis pain differs from the everyday stomach upset many people notice when they start a GLP-1 drug. It is usually intense and steady rather than mild and passing. It often centers in the upper abdomen. It may get worse after eating. Some people also develop a fever, a rapid pulse or a swollen, tender belly.

Doctors usually confirm the condition with a blood test that measures pancreatic enzymes such as lipase and amylase. Imaging, such as a CT scan or an ultrasound, can show inflammation and help rule out other causes. Acute pancreatitis typically needs hospital care. Treatment includes intravenous fluids, pain control and a break from eating while the pancreas recovers.

Other factors raise pancreatitis risk on their own. Gallstones and heavy alcohol use are the two leading causes of acute pancreatitis. Very high triglyceride levels are another. Several of the GLP-1 labels note that the drugs have not been studied in people with a past history of pancreatitis. That history is worth raising with a prescriber before treatment begins.

Anyone taking a GLP-1 drug who develops severe abdominal pain that does not go away should seek prompt medical care.

Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, is a sudden loss of vision caused by reduced blood flow to the optic nerve. In June 2025, the European Medicines Agency's safety committee concluded that it is a very rare side effect of semaglutide, affecting up to 1 in 10,000 people.

That committee is the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee, known as PRAC. It reviews safety signals for medicines sold in the European Union. Its conclusion covers semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus. It does not establish the same risk for tirzepatide or other GLP-1 drugs.

Very rare is the lowest defined frequency band in European medicine labeling. It sits below the common, uncommon and rare categories. That placement is why NAION closes this list.

The optic nerve carries visual signals from the eye to the brain. In NAION, the front of that nerve, where it joins the back of the eye, loses part of its blood supply. The starved nerve fibers stop passing signals properly.

The condition usually strikes one eye. The loss is typically painless and is often noticed on waking. People may see blurring, dimming or a dark shadow. That shadow often covers the upper or lower half of the visual field.

The term non-arteritic separates it from arteritic optic neuropathy. That form is caused by giant cell arteritis, an inflammation of blood vessels. Doctors use an eye examination and blood tests to tell the two apart.

Vision lost to NAION often does not fully return. No treatment has been proven to restore it reliably. In some people, the second eye is affected later.

NAION also occurs in people who take no medication at all. Recognized risk factors include diabetes, high blood pressure, obstructive sleep apnea and a small, crowded optic disc. Type 2 diabetes is the condition Ozempic and Rybelsus are prescribed to treat.

A sudden drop in vision while taking a GLP-1 drug is a reason to seek emergency eye care. An eye specialist can examine the optic nerve directly. Patients should tell the examining doctor which medication they take and when they started it.

#5456. Anthropic debuts Claude Fable, Mythos 5.2 models, priced 20% below OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra

Anthropic debuted Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on Monday, the company’s answer to OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, which came out in early September.

The new models, which could be Anthropic’s last big releases before its IPO, claim to offer higher performance than Astra at a lower price point—a key factor for earning and retaining customers in a world where professionals seem quick to switch to models based on cost, as long as the performance holds up.

The launch is critical for Anthropic as it seeks to re-accelerate revenue growth, following a third quarter slowdown revealed in latest S-1 filing with the SEC.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are 20% cheaper than Astra for ordinary input and output tasks, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, compared to $10 and $50, respectively, for GPT-6 Astra. Tokens are the unit of information AI model process. One token of English language text is equivalent to about a word-and-a-half. For prompts with large amounts of information, such as documents, the cost advantage is more pronounced. Anthropic’s new models are 80% cheaper, at 20 cents per million cached tokens compared to one dollar per million cached tokens for GPT-6 Astra.

Anthropic reports impressive results from its pre-release testing. The new models “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications,” the company said.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 perform better than its competitors on coding evaluation benchmarks, Anthropic said, noting that over 90% of the company’s own code is written by AI. While Anthropic’s Claude Code product gained an early lead among programmers, OpenAI’s Codex has gained ground in recent months due to its lower pricing, The Information reported in late October. The combination of lower pricing plus superior performance, if the company’s claims hold up in real-world testing, could help win them back.

The new models are best when used for the “most ambitious, open-ended technical work,” Anthropic said. In other words, they’re competing with Astra at the frontier. However, for daily tasks, Anthropic recommends its customers use its more cost-effective model, Opus 5.5. That model is more expensive than its direct competitor from OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Sol, although it still could end up being a better deal if it yields a high quality result more often. That’s for users to decide as they inevitably begin to try Anthropic’s latest releases and weigh options on a daily basis.

Anthropic is also trying to compete with OpenAI on cybersecurity tasks, such as finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code. The company claims an unnamed security company “found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested.” Late last week, OpenAI debuted a cybersecurity-focused model, GPT-6 Cyber.

The new Anthropic models also reportedly solved two theoretical physics problems related to black holes, and identified a way to speed up research into gene therapies. In light of OpenAI making headlines for solving mathematics proofs that have eluded academics for decades—most notably the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem—Anthropic is highlighting its new models’ mathematics chops as well.

A team of 1,000 agents powerd by Fable 5.2 produced a formalization, or translation of a mathematical proof into a format a computer can check step by step, in 30 hours, compared with 11 days for a previous, unreleased research version of Claude. In a subtle jab at the mathematics community’s backlash to OpenAI pouring millions of dollars into solving proofs and upending the field, Anthropic notes that its quick formalizations can help human mathematicians check their proofs faster so they can “spend more time exploring novel ideas.”

One unique area Anthropic seems to be leaning into more than OpenAI is hardware and robotics. The new models were allegedly able to design and produce three working electronic devices, complete with circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software, based on a one-paragraph prompt.

Finally, Anthropic highlighted the models’ safety features, including safeguards that block “high-risk cyber activities including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology.”

Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Mythos 5.2 access is application-only for cybersecurity professionals and life sciences researchers. Claude Enterprise customers can also access Mythos 5.2 through Anthropic’s Claude Security product.

#5455. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5454. California Wine Country Saw Its Earliest Harvest in Decades. Here’s How a 67-Year-Old Business Navigated It — And What Every Entrepreneur Can Learn.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From supply chain to sustainability, Rodney Strong Vineyards knows what it takes to succeed.

Napa Valley and Sonoma, two of California’s top-growing wine regions, recently underwent their earliest grape harvest in decades. In response to a record-breaking March heat wave and early bud break, grape-picking started in July. The process typically starts in early to mid-August.

Fortunately, wine-growers and -makers across the region turn to harvest playbooks that have withstood the test of time.

One of them is 67-year-old Rodney Strong Vineyards in Healdsburg, California.

Rodney Strong, who had a brief stint in the Navy before dancing on Broadway in New York City, retired from performing life and established his namesake winery in 1959. He brought on Rick Sayre as winemaker in 1979.

In 1989, the Klein family purchased Rodney Strong Vineyards. A graduate of Stanford’s MBA program, Tom Klein met Strong and Sayre a decade prior when his team at McKinsey & Company was hired to evaluate the winery.

To this day, more than six decades on, a successful harvest at Rodney Strong Vineyards strikes the balance between art and science. (Just one example of many: The preferred light pink shade of Rodney Strong’s rosé requires bringing those grapes in under the cover of night, before any heat can degrade them).

During the final days of 2026’s harvest, Entrepreneur visited Rodney Strong Vineyards and its estate vineyard Rockaway Vineyards to learn more about the business’s approach.

The takeaways from chief winemaking and operations officer Justin Seidenfeld and head of winegrowing Allison Dericco can ripen any business for success, whether or not they’re focused on the vine.

Businesses should never underestimate the value of knowing their supply chain — and its nuances — to ensure their product delivers on quality every time.

On the topic of Rodney Strong’s very intentional rosé: Heat is the most immediate logistical risk to grape quality between a morning harvest at Rockaway Vineyards and the crush pad.

“As the fruit sits in the sun, it will begin to dessicate,” Seidenfeld says. “That will change the balance of the fruit.”

That’s why the team starts picking grapes at dawn and fast tracks them to the winery. The fruit is kept in an air-conditioned space until it’s sorted and put into a tank for fermentation, Seidenfeld notes.

These days, businesses across industries can drill down on their supply chain with advanced technologies that gather data at every touchpoint, putting an innovative twist on operational fundamentals that comes with a major competitive advantage.

In a similar vein, businesses have to understand their assets and how to prioritize them for long-term success.

Rodney Strong boasts a robust wine portfolio. A premium, small-lot Rockaway grape experiences a different crush and fermentation than a larger-lot grape destined for the broader Sonoma County or Estate tiers.

Rodney Strong’s Sonoma and Estate wines are larger, so they require a less precise “sweet spotting” technique compared to Rockaway and other reserve wines, Seidenfeld says.

Still, those grapes destined for the broader tier are managed closely to ensure quality.

“[We rely on] careful site development to keep the block as uniform as possible and the implantation of deficit irrigation to help find as much balance across the whole block as possible,” Seidenfeld says.

What’s more, any business can put this into practice by zeroing in on an often overlooked strategy: dynamic resource allocation, which shifts money, talent and management attention to areas where they can generate the most value.

Data analysis plays an important role in business operations and risk mitigation, but well-informed intuition can be just as valuable.

At the vineyard, whether a block of grapes hangs on the vine for one more day or gets picked as soon as possible comes down to chemistry and gut feeling.

Seidenfeld says the decision on when to harvest is the most important one the winery makes every year.

“While we use the data from the samples we pull to guide us, the final call on when to harvest is made through our eyes and ears and taste and not with what we get from the lab,” Seidenfeld explains.

Some degree of risk is inevitable in business, but entrepreneurs who pay attention to the pressures related to growth, culture and information management can sharpen their decision-making ability when it counts — and minimize potential losses.

Businesses that embrace sustainability not only foster positive consumer sentiment, but also protect their long-term product viability and bottom line.

Rodney Strong became the first carbon neutral winery in Sonoma County in 2009. The team works to create a balanced growing environment with practices like water conservation, soil management and biodiversity encouragement, maintaining healthy vines and managing stress as they develop, Dericco notes.

Additionally, using tools like soil moisture monitoring, weather stations and plant-based measurements allows the team to make more precise farming decisions, particularly when it comes to irrigation.

“While our carbon neutrality and waste reduction efforts have broader environmental benefits, it’s these everyday practices in the vineyard that directly influence vine health, fruit development, and ultimately, wine quality,” Dericco says.

The lesson for business owners? Consider sustainability a building block, not an afterthought, to ensure genuine messaging and meaningful collaboration.

#5453. Vietnam’s cheap coffee may lose its edge as the EU tightens sustainability rules, Nestlé Vietnam’s chair warns

Vietnam’s cheap coffee is “no longer going to be attractive to export” as the European Union tightens its sustainability rules, Binu Jacob, chairman and managing director of Nestlé Vietnam, warned last week at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Ho Chi Minh City on Nov. 3.

The Southeast Asian nation is the world’s second-largest coffee producer and the largest producer of robusta, the variety largely used in instant coffee. Europe is the world’s largest coffee market, accounting for about 24% of global consumption, according to the European Coffee Federation. That gives the bloc’s standards outsized importance for producers.

“Vietnam was always known to produce cheap coffee, but cheap coffee is no longer going to be attractive to export because [the] EU is coming up with very stringent norms,” Jacob said. “So if we don’t go up the value chain and create coffee that is sustainable and that meets the very high standards, we will be unable to export.”

The EU Deforestation Regulation applies to most companies from Dec. 30, 2026, though some smaller businesses will not need to comply until later in 2027. The regulation aims to curb deforestation and forest degradation linked to the production of certain commodities, and to reduce the bloc’s contribution to greenhouse gas emissions and biodiversity loss.

Hanoi is working with Brussels on compliance. The multiyear, EU-backed SustainCoffee project aims to help the country’s coffee sector meet international environmental, social, and governance standards, and support more than 400 coffee-related businesses while indirectly benefit an estimated 1.4 million farmers and workers in the supply chain.

Nestlé has applied its global research and development capabilities, partnering with the Western Highlands Agriculture and Forestry Science Institute, a prominent agricultural research institution, to develop a coffee plantlet “best suited for the soil conditions in the Central Highlands,” Jacob said.

The company propagates the plantlets through tissue culture. “From one leaf of this coffee plant, you can actually make 2,000 trees, and this is what we’ve been doing in the last 15 years,” he explained.

“We have made 100 million plantlets of this disease-resistant coffee plantlet, and then distributed it at subsidized rates to farmers all over central Vietnam,” he said. “As a result, the productivity and the yield of coffee today in Vietnam is three times that of the global average, and this can be replicated anywhere in the world.”

Still, Jacob cast the rules as a chance for Vietnam to move up the value chain. “With small farms, it’s quite easy to move from the old ways of traditional farming to regenerative farming,” he said. “Once you do that, Vietnam has a competitive advantage to export more and ensure that more value stays here.”

#5452. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5451. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5450. Nvidia built itself around one man. A scandal is testing that bet

Few executives loom larger over a single company than Jensen Huang does at Nvidia. His 33-year reign as CEO, and the success he’s overseen during the AI boom, have made him a hugely powerful force at the $4.3 trillion company. Now, the linchpin of the AI industry will test the limits of its corporate governance and succession planning.

After Huang on Sunday acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, Nvidia’s board announced an investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The admission followed reporting about his relationship with a woman whom U.S. authorities concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times. The board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that its inquiry would examine “all available information.”

The trick for investigators, according to business and law experts, is that they are investigating, and will potentially consider ousting, perhaps the most critical executive to America’s AI success. And they will do so under a company power structure in which Huang reigns as an outsized decision-maker.

Huang is “synonymous with Nvidia, and Nvidia is synonymous with him, and he and Nvidia are synonymous with AI, so he’s bound up in the company’s identity much more than other cases,” Brian Burke, founder of Burke Law & Strategy and a corporate board advisor, told Fortune. Nvidia is “a paradigm out there that people look up to and they say, ‘Oh, I want to be like Nvidia.’ Other CEOs say, ‘I want to be like Jensen Huang.’ So, it’s really almost like a cult.”

Huang, 63, has set up a unique structure around him at Nvidia that has concentrated decision-making in his hands. He has been CEO for 33 years, astonishingly long for any company. Nvidia has no chief operating officer, and Huang has about 60 direct reports, creating uncertainty about who is next in line to lead.

Huang is known to play a central role in strategic and technical decisions, and the success he’s had since the AI boom got underway in late 2022 has only strengthened his grip on the company and the AI industry at large. He has become something of a celebrity in the tech world, with followers wearing leather jackets to copy him and fans pursuing him at corporate events for a selfie or a signature. He has also gotten close to the Trump administration, which has counted on him for counsel on AI and taken him on foreign trips.

Huang is Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, with a 3.56% stake, but he doesn’t have any super-voting shares like Mark Zuckerberg has at Meta Platforms. He leads what is the world’s second most valuable company. (Its shares sank more than 4% on Monday after he admitted to the affaire.) Nvidia has been estimated to control about 90% of the market for high-powered GPU computer chips used in AI data centers.

The company has also operated without a chief compliance officer. In a September 2022 staff at the Securities and Exchange Commission asked for more detail about board risk oversight, whether the company had such an officer and to whom that person reported, and about its overall structure. Nvidia has said it has a compliance committee made up of its chief financial officer, executive vice president of operations, and senior vice president of human resources, which it says “ensures communication of and adherence to all NVIDIA policies.”

There are few other cases, if any, that resemble Nvidia’s current situation. Corporate executives whose romantic liaisons have derailed their careers are common enough. In 2019, McDonald’s fired CEO Steve Easterbrook over a consensual relationship with an employee that violated company policy. The bigger scandal came afterward: the company discovered additional undisclosed relationships, sued to recover his exit compensation, and ultimately recovered cash and equity valued at $105 million. In this case however, the romantic liaison involves an alleged spy and the CEO of the dominant company building some of the U.S.’s most valuable technology.

Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University who has studied CEO succession practices, told Fortune that Nvidia’s concentration of so much power and decision-making in Huang now makes it very vulnerable to what comes next.

“The board has made a mistake by not having a clearly outlined succession plan that’s been telegraphed to the market for a year or two,” Schloetzer said. “They find themselves at the day of reckoning, and it’s a sudden and perhaps forced one, rather than a relay situation where they have time to figure it out as they go.”

Hui Chen, a former federal prosecutor who served as the U.S. Justice Department’s first compliance counsel expert from 2015 to 2017, told Fortune that corporate risk efforts tend to focus on leaks from rank and file staff members, and companies don’t pay as much attention to similar risks by high-level executives.

Schloetzer and other experts said it’s plausible for the board to appoint an interim CEO or have Nvidia’s lead independent director—Stephen Neal, chairman emeritus and senior counsel at law firm Cooley LLP—as interim CEO if Huang steps down. Another option for an interim could be Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress. The concern with any next-CEO plan is how the market will receive the decision, since Huang is seen as critical to Nvidia’s success.

Huang also has children who work at Nvidia and could be options to succeed him. Spencer Huang is a director of product management, and his daughter, Madison, is a senior director of product marketing. Both have reportedly worked on robotics at the company. His son-in-law, Nico Caprez, is vice president of global AI infrastructure growth.

The board could oust Huang at the end of its investigation, or Huang could have to step down before then, Burke said. He could also leave the CEO role but stay on in another capacity.

In media interviews over the years, Huang has dismissed conventional succession planning, saying his approach is to continually transfer his knowledge to colleagues. He has also said he hopes Nvidia’s next CEO already works at the company, even though Nvidia has not publicly identified a successor.

#5449. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.
