#5352. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party."

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

#5351. Rich Dad Poor Dad Author Anticipates Bitcoin's Next Crash

Amid the growing fear surrounding the sustained crypto market downturn, Robert Kiyosaki, the author of Rich Dad Poor Dad, has triggered discussions after airing his own opinion.

While the rest of the market remains in panic, Kiyosaki has issued a statement earlier today, declaring that he is even anticipating the next Bitcoin crash.

Unlike most crypto investors, Kiyosaki has confidently expressed that he sees market downturns as opportunities to expand his portfolio at cheaper costs.

Kiyosaki mentioned that while other investors were panicking amid the recent market volatility that saw Bitcoin retest previous lows, he had bought more Bitcoin, gold, and silver instead.

His statement does not entirely come as a surprise, as Kiyosaki is well known as one of the most legendary crypto investors with unwavering confidence in Bitcoin and other physical assets like gold and silver.

However, he triggered further debate after comparing the falling prices of these assets with other economic crises, noting that they are bigger threats.

While Kiyosaki questioned the crypto community about the growing fear and panic over Bitcoin's falling price, he suggested that they should be more concerned about the growing global debt, especially in the United States.

Kiyosaki further highlighted that the bigger threats investors are supposed to be worried about are the growing debt burden, poor leadership across many nations, and the traditional education system that has failed to teach people about money and financial management.

#5350. RLUSD Is Not Coming for XRP: Garlinghouse Clarifies Ripple’s Bigger XRPL Vision as Trader Spots Setup Behind 71% Price Explosion

Ripple CEO Bradley Garlinghouse is pushing back against the idea that the company’s growing RLUSD stablecoin ambitions come at XRP’s expense, insisting the stablecoin is targeting a different market altogether.

As Ripple sharpens its vision for the XRP Ledger, a separate development is drawing attention to XRP’s price prospects, with prominent crypto trader Ali Charts spotting a chart pattern that previously preceded a staggering 71% rally.

Garlinghouse sees the RLUSD stablecoin as a way to bring more activity and practical use cases to the XRP Ledger, not as a competitor to XRP. Instead of treating the stablecoin as a rival, he framed its growth as part of the broader momentum behind XRP, arguing that both assets can play complementary roles in expanding the ecosystem.

“RLUSD isn’t competing with XRP. It’s competing with other stablecoins. Use case matters, and I want those use cases running on the XRPL,” Garlinghouse wrote on X.

By targeting the wider market, Ripple hopes to expand the range of financial applications operating on its blockchain. Garlinghouse emphasized that the company wants RLUSD-powered use cases to run on XRPL, potentially attracting more businesses, developers, and institutional users to the network.

Garlinghouse was responding to XRP community researcher WrathofKahneman, who argued that RLUSD’s expansion could ultimately benefit XRP by increasing liquidity across the XRP Ledger. “RLUSD is great for XRP. More XRPL liquidity makes XRP easier to use in the long run & it isn’t replacing XRP where it wasn’t used,” the researcher wrote.

However, WrathofKahneman cautioned that the benefits may not immediately translate into significant price gains without direct demand for XRP. “The problem is that w/out direct use, price impact is 2nd order,” he added.

The researcher also raised a broader question about XRP’s future role in the ecosystem: “Will XRP become a specialized institutional asset with gated liquidity, or be ubiquitous?”

Agreed! RLUSD isn’t competing with XRP. It’s competing with other stablecoins. Use case matters, and I want those use cases running on the XRPL.

The debate is particularly relevant as XRP trades around $1.28, well below its previous all-time high of $3.65, even as Ripple continues to expand its institutional footprint. While growing adoption could strengthen the XRP Ledger, investors are still watching to see whether that progress will translate into stronger demand and sustained price appreciation for XRP.

Meanwhile, crypto analyst Ali Charts has identified a potentially bullish technical signal on XRP’s four-hour chart, suggesting the token could be gearing up for another significant move. According to the analyst, XRP recently recorded its tightest Bollinger Band squeeze since August before breaking above the upper band, which could signal building upward momentum.

The setup is drawing attention because a similar period of extreme volatility compression preceded an impressive rally earlier this year. Ali Charts noted that the last time XRP’s Bollinger Bands were this tightly compressed, the token surged nearly 71% in just three days.

The pundit believes another parabolic price move could now be taking shape. At its current price of around $1.16, a repeat of the previous 71% surge would push XRP to approximately $2.19. Such a move would represent a substantial recovery for the token, potentially bringing it closer to key resistance levels and reigniting bullish sentiment across the XRP market.

Traders will be watching whether XRP can sustain its move above the upper Bollinger Band and attract enough buying pressure to confirm a breakout. However, a failure to hold the gains could turn the latest bullish signal into another false start.

Corporate America, in the person of Apple, is defending its sovereignty in the home market, but the offshore market will not be stopped by this.

#5347. ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

American Riot Platforms Inc. (RIOT) sold off 79% of its Bitcoin in the third quarter of 2026, redirecting capital toward building infrastructure for artificial intelligence. According to a fresh financial report, the company reduced its cryptocurrency reserves from 11,380 to 2,418 BTC.

In total, over the first nine months of the year, Riot sold 20,264 BTC on the market, receiving about $1.5 billion for them. This money went toward financing a major technological shift: the company's free energy capacity is being repurposed for high-performance computing needs.

Riot shares reacted to the session open with a sharp jump to $16.20, after which they stabilized in the $15.45–$15.50 range, holding positions on elevated volumes.

The main incentive for selling the cryptocurrency was a 15-year agreement to lease ready-made sites and capacities (powered land lease) totaling 910 MW at the Corsicana campus in Texas. The strategic partner was the Frontier AI Lab (Anthropic) laboratory.

The initial cost of the contract is estimated at $28 billion, and the average annual rent at the start will be about $1.8 billion. Taking into account other projects, Riot's total long-term revenue in the data center segment has reached $38 billion, and the total controlled capacity is 1,151 MW.

Riot CEO Jason Les noted that the agreement is structured as a triple-net lease. Under its terms, the client itself purchases and maintains the computing equipment. For Riot, this reduces construction costs by roughly half compared to standard Tier 3 data centers. As a result, the company will be able to do without issuing new shares and diluting investors' stakes.

The shift in focus is occurring against the backdrop of falling margins in classic mining. Riot's quarterly revenue from cryptocurrency mining fell by 28% — to $116 million, although the company actually mined 1,637 BTC.

Nevertheless, total quarterly revenue held at $181.4 million (+1% year-over-year), outpacing market forecasts. Net profit amounted to $4.03 million.

To optimize its balance sheet, the company fully closed its $200 million credit line with Coinbase, returning 5,821 BTC from collateral. Riot ended the quarter with free liquidity of $950.2 million (including cash and the remainder of the cryptocurrency). The balance sheet retains 2,418 BTC, which may also go under the hammer in the fourth quarter to finance the Texas construction.

#5345. XRP Ledger Activates New Amendment to Strengthen Network

The XRP Ledger (XRPL) network recently activated a new amendment that helps secure the network by resolving potential security weaknesses and making some existing functionalities more robust and reliable.

This latest amendment, called fixCleanup3_4_0, was activated on Nov. 4, bringing a series of technical updates that include fixes for token issuance, automated market makers (AMMs), lending functionalities, and other parts of the XRP Ledger network.

A fix for a potential security weak point related to token issuance on the XRP Ledger network is a critical aspect of the latest amendment.

As explained in the official documentation of the XRP Ledger network, this update addresses a potential weakness related to delegated permissions that could allow some accounts to issue tokens when they are only allowed to destroy them.

On the XRP Ledger, token issuers can grant permissions to other accounts to perform certain tasks. For example, a stablecoin issuer could delegate permission to burn tokens to another account when customers want to redeem them.

With the latest amendment, the XRP Ledger network addresses this security weakness by preventing a zero-balance, burn-only delegated payment from resulting in the issuance of new tokens.

On top of addressing token issuance permissions, there's more to the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment.

As explained in the official XRP Ledger network documentation, the fixCleanup3_4_0 update brings several fixes to decentralized trading, asset management, and transaction processing.

For automated market makers (AMMs), this latest update prevents some invalid auction bids and makes some improvements to how liquidity withdrawals and token clawbacks work.

It also brings some fixes for potential unexpected calculation errors or rounding issues that could occur in some cases.

These changes are supposed to make things more predictable when it comes to liquidity pools and avoid potential failures that could happen in some cases.

Another significant aspect of these changes concerns Single Asset Vaults and the proposed native lending infrastructure on the XRP Ledger.

As explained, this amendment brings some improvements to how rounding is handled when assets enter or exit vaults.

The idea is to ensure that transactions do not result in more or fewer assets being transferred than they should.

#5344. Ripple Executive Reveals Massive Growth of Company's London Hub

According to Ripple's UK and Europe Managing Director, Cassie Craddock, Ripple’s London office has expanded significantly over the last decade to become Ripple’s largest international hub outside the U.S.

“When we moved into our current office in 2018, there were 2 floors, and a lot of empty desks. Now we’re on 3 floors and full on all the desks. We’re now over capacity,” she wrote on X.

Craddock's comments came after she took part in a fireside chat at the British Residence in New York as part of Ripple’s Swell conference.

She revealed that Ripple chose to focus on London early on, given the UK's strong capital markets, mature legal system, experienced regulators and concentration of financial talent.

However, she added that regulatory uncertainty had previously limited the company’s capacity to build more relationships with leading U.K. financial institutions.

Ripple's story in the U.K. capital began on March 21, 2016, when the San Francisco-based company officially announced the launch of its first office in London, located in Canary Wharf.

Back then, the expansion was meant to accommodate the growing interest of European banks in distributed ledger technology and cross-border settlement solutions.

Ripple incorporated its U.K. entity in April 2016 under the name Ripple Europe Ltd. (later changed to Ripple Markets UK Ltd. in August 2022).

Ripple continued to expand its ties to U.K. financial institutions in the following years.

In April 2018, Santander introduced its new international payments app, One Pay FX, which used Ripple’s xCurrent technology.

In February 2022, Ripple announced a partnership with London-based payments company Modulr to make it easier to send cross-border payments to the UK and Europe.

Moreover, Ripple has played a role in developing the research landscape for blockchain in the U.K. In January 2026, Ripple shared that it had pledged more than £5M to UK universities under its University Blockchain Research Initiative.

One of the major milestones for Ripple in the U.K. occurred on Jan. 9, when Ripple received an Electronic Money Institution license and cryptoasset registration from the Financial Conduct Authority. The authorizations enabled Ripple to extend its regulated cross-border payment services to UK institutions.

In February, Ripple also secured a partnership with Aviva Investors to explore the tokenization of traditional investment funds.

This work resulted in the launch of a tokenized share class of Aviva Investors’ £22bn Sterling Liquidity Fund on the XRP Ledger on Oct. 26.

#5343. Solana Targets Durable Nonces After $270M Drift Hack as Pump.fun Backlash Grows

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Solana developers are preparing to remove durable nonces, the transaction feature exploited in April’s $270 million Drift Protocol hack. The proposed change marks a major shift in how the network handles offline approvals, with implications for exchanges and institutional custodians.

The proposal, known as SIMD-0723, would retire a mechanism that allows signed transactions to remain valid indefinitely. Attackers reportedly exploited this functionality to execute pre-approved transactions more than a week after obtaining signatures from Drift’s security council.

Solana wants to kill the feature behind April's $270M+ Drift hack.SIMD-0723, filed Nov 5 by Anza, would retire "durable nonces": signed transactions that never expire. Normal Solana transactions go stale in ~30 seconds. Earliest switch-off: May 5, 2027. pic.twitter.com/VYYttCsvJk

The move comes as Solana faces another challenge closer to its retail ecosystem. Pump.fun is facing growing community criticism over platform fees, influencer promotions, and allegations of hidden-wallet trading. Together, the developments put renewed attention on security, transparency and trust across Solana’s ecosystem.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Normal Solana transactions use recent blockhashes that expire after 30 seconds. Durable nonces replace those temporary references with stored values, allowing transactions to remain executable until the nonce advances.

The feature was designed for legitimate operational needs. Exchanges, custodians, and multisig organizations often require offline signing procedures that take longer than Solana’s normal transaction window.

However, attackers turned that convenience into an attack vector against Drift on April 1, 2026. They reportedly secured administrative approvals through air-gapped signing systems before allowing the transactions to sit for more than a week.

Once submitted, the approvals helped attackers take control of the protocol and drain at least $270 million. Drift subsequently attributed the attack to a North Korean-linked group.

Anza contributor Gabe Rodriguez filed SIMD-0723 on November 5. The proposal would require transactions to use recent blockhashes after activation. May 5, 2027, represents the earliest proposed mainnet activation date. The change still requires technical approval and migration planning.

Solana is also exploring replacement programs that could support offline signing without relying on durable nonces. These alternatives would introduce different authorization and transaction-failure considerations for custodians.

The proposal forces institutional users to reconsider how they authorize transactions across Solana. Meanwhile, questions about trust are becoming harder to ignore elsewhere in the ecosystem.

Pump.fun has attracted fresh criticism following several developments involving its business model and influencer ecosystem.

On November 6, blockchain tracker Lookonchain reported that Pump.fun transferred 76,111 SOL, worth approximately $6.85 million, to Kraken. The movement reignited criticism over platform fees and whether its incentives adequately serve ordinary traders.

Pump fun(@Pumpfun) is dumping $SOL again!They just deposited 76,111 $SOL ($6.85M) into #Kraken.In total, https://t.co/TcwYRTArT2 has sold 5,553,833 $SOL($882.4M) at an average price of $158.88.https://t.co/kyztoJLCjt pic.twitter.com/QvzqaR8fGI

Bubblemaps also accused prominent influencers of using undisclosed wallets to purchase tokens before publicly recommending them. Its investigations estimated $125,000 in combined trading profits and promotional rewards involving influencer Ethan.

Separate allegations involving paid streamer collaborations surfaced on November 7. The revelations have intensified questions about transparency within Pump.fun’s promotional ecosystem.

These controversies involve different problems from Drift’s exploit, but they expose a similar challenge: maintaining confidence among participants.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

That challenge also creates an interesting opportunity for Bitcoin-focused projects exploring alternative execution environments.

Bitcoin Hyper is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 using Solana Virtual Machine technology. Its architecture aims to combine SVM’s high-speed execution with Bitcoin-based settlement, bringing smart contracts, decentralized exchanges, and staking functionality to BTC.

Bitcoin Hyper is not simply another Solana application. Its design uses SVM execution while anchoring Layer 2 state to Bitcoin through periodic commitments and zero-knowledge proofs.

This combination gives it a different proposition from Solana-native applications. Developers can work with an execution environment associated with Solana’s performance, while the project targets Bitcoin’s established settlement infrastructure.

Bitcoin Hyper has also reached several development milestones. Its testnet is live, with a public explorer allowing users to inspect transactions and network activity.

The project’s presale has raised approximately $33.2 million, with HYPER priced at a low $0.0136 per coin. Its November 26 presale deadline leaves 17 days from today for prospective participants to enter before the planned launch window.

The upcoming transition toward mainnet, wallet infrastructure, and exchange listings puts the project in an important stage of development. Its combination of Bitcoin settlement and SVM execution gives it a distinct position in the expanding Bitcoin Layer 2 sector.

Perplexity AI predicts what the US CPI data may read and, if so, what could potentially happen to Bitcoin and the broader market. CPI data remains one of the most market-moving economic releases for both stocks and crypto. The next one is in two days, on November 10, and both crypto and the stock market seem to be waiting to see which direction it goes from here.

Traditionally, a cooler-than-expected Consumer Price Index print is bullish for risk assets. Lower inflation reduces pressure on the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates elevated or hike them further, which supports lower Treasury yields, a softer dollar, and higher valuations for growth-oriented assets.

The inflation rate increased in September on the back of higher gasoline and energy prices amid the Iran war, further squeezing households’ budgets and perhaps pressuring the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, economists said.

The consumer price index rose by 3.7% in September from 12 months earlier, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. That’s up from 3.4% annually in August.

September’s report came in hotter than expected, triggering an immediate sell-off across cryptocurrency and broader risk-asset markets.

Bitcoin slid from roughly $83,900–$84,000 down toward $81,000–$81,500, hitting lows around $80,210 in subsequent early trading sessions.

The total cryptocurrency market capitalization compressed to $2.7 trillion, accompanied by over $160M in leveraged long liquidations within a 24-hour window following the October 14 CPI data drop.

Crypto often amplifies this reaction: Bitcoin and major altcoins historically perform well in environments of easing monetary expectations because they benefit from improved liquidity conditions and renewed risk appetite.

Conversely, a hotter-than-expected CPI reading typically pressures stocks and crypto lower, reinforcing a “higher-for-longer” rates narrative, strengthening the dollar, and lifting yields.

For the October 2026 CPI data due Tuesday, November 10 at 8:30 a.m. ET, current market consensus points to a clear cooling from September’s strong print.

Economists surveyed by Bloomberg and other sources expect headline CPI to rise 0.3% month-over-month (down from +0.6% previously), with core CPI (excluding food and energy) advancing 0.2% MoM (down from +0.3%).

Some forecasts cluster slightly lower around 0.2–0.25% for headline. Year-over-year figures are complicated by prior data gaps, but the monthly numbers are the primary focus.

Sentiment leans toward a soft-to-in-line outcome that would confirm inflation is decelerating after two firmer months, though markets remain sensitive to any upside surprise in core services or shelter components.

While not a dramatic undershoot, it would land on the dovish side of the range. If this prediction materializes, risk assets should react positively. Treasury yields would likely dip, the dollar could soften, and both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would find support for a relief rally.

Crypto would stand to benefit disproportionately in the short term, with Bitcoin potentially extending recent recovery gains and higher-beta alts seeing stronger percentage moves as liquidity expectations improve.

A confirmatory soft print would also increase the odds that the Federal Reserve maintains a more patient stance into the December meeting, reducing near-term hawkish risks.

However, the market impact would still depend on the details, particularly the composition of core inflation, and any accompanying commentary on sticky services categories. Overall, a result in line with or slightly below the Perplexity forecast would reinforce the recent post-midterm risk-on tone rather than derail it.

#5340. Crypto’s Next Two Years Should Be About Survival, Not Competition: Vitalik Buterin

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has warned crypto executives to switch focus to collective security and survival rather than competition between platforms. This follows multiple hacks that drained billions from the market and crushed traders’ sentiment.

In an interview with MoneyControl, Buterin urged crypto executives to focus on protecting user assets as a collective, as that could shape how regulators approach the sector. The next couple of years are key, as frameworks are still expected in several jurisdictions.

Digital asset firms, particularly centralized exchanges, have focused on gaining a larger share of the market cap, onboarding more users, etc but this buzz around gains leaves room for bad actors. For Buterin, the actions in the next couple of years will determine the long-term roadmap.

Most crypto users agreed with the Ethereum executive because, without asset safety, centralized exchanges will see capital exodus and more backing from traditional finance firms.

Recently, several crypto companies were hacked, including Binance, the largest centralized exchange by trading volume. Bad actors flagged in North Korea drained $6 billion; although large parts were recovered, it still remains the largest crypto hack of all time.

This week, Brazil’s largest exchange, Mercado, also suffered a breach that temporarily suspended trading. In a nutshell, these losses could prompt regulators to tighten requirements, setting the sector back.

Previously, regulators in the US and Europe often cited investor-protection concerns to delay major developments that would open the sector to traditional capital. Notably, spot crypto ETFs are a top example, although things changed after the White House backed the move following President Trump’s election win.

Buterin also added that recent attacks now target user interfaces and centralized components rather than smart contracts. He called for more operations to move on-chain, citing Binance Smart Chain and others.

“One good decision that Binance made is that they also launched Binance Smart Chain. They also benefit from the fact that if you do things with contracts on-chain, you can have very high levels of security. I am expecting we’re going to see more moves in that direction.”

On Ethereum security, Buterin and developers rolled out a roadmap to protect assets ahead of Q-Day. The network is lauded for taking early steps ahead of others as supercomputers get more powerful.

#5339. webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight users want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card shows the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 new tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

The card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

The useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

#5338. Binance's CZ Sounds Alarm Over New Crypto Phishing Scam

Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) has warned about a malicious crypto phishing scheme that uses a fake Trust Wallet website to lure unsuspecting users into connecting their wallets.

CZ shared a warning about a fraudulent website with a fake domain that mimics the popular Trust Wallet website.

Attackers modified the website domain by replacing the “u” with “a” and changing the extension from “.com” to “.cam,” which may trick unsuspecting users who don’t carefully inspect the domain.

The malicious website tricks users into connecting their crypto wallets in order to review their transfers.

However, the site contains JavaScript code that attempts to scan wallet balances using a backend API in order to prepare transfers to specific wallet addresses.

The attacker’s setup works with multiple well-known crypto wallets such as Trust Wallet, Phantom, and OKX Wallet.

CZ’s warning comes shortly after a surge in crypto phishing attempts against wallet users.

On Nov. 3, cybersecurity firm Bitdefender announced that scammers had started using the recent Binance security breach to spread fake emails impersonating Trust Wallet.

The phishing emails suggested that Trust Wallet users were also impacted by the Binance security breach. Therefore, they instructed users to perform a mandatory wallet verification procedure.

The email messages warned that users would be suspended after Nov. 7 if they did not complete the wallet verification process.

Bitdefender said that the phishing scheme affected users in multiple countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and South Africa.

The phishing messages led users to fake verification websites where their wallet credentials or recovery data could be leaked.

Earlier this year, cybersecurity analysts from CYFIRMA spotted another phishing attack against Trust Wallet users. The attackers used malicious QR codes on Telegram to target Trust Wallet users.

Bitcoin closed the week below its 50-week moving average for the first time in two months, just as warnings grow that the calm in the oil market may not last.

The weekly candle closed at $74,851 at midnight UTC on Sunday. That is below the 50-week simple moving average (MA), the average of the last 50 weekly closes, which sits at $75,535. It was also the fifth losing week in a row, and BTC trades at $74,312 on Binance on Monday morning.

Oil has gone the other way. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell 17% from $117.64 on October 30 to $97.35 this morning, as traders bet on a deal to end the war with Iran.

That bet may be early. Amos Hochstein was an energy adviser to President Joe Biden. He told CNBC that the risk of renewed war is “still alive.” If fighting resumes, he said, gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel prices would all surge.

So if oil spikes again, does BTC fall further?

The drop came fast. Brent lost 10.9% on Monday, November 2, and another 8.7% on Wednesday, as traders bet that the fighting would end.

No deal has been signed. Late Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it had disabled a tanker that ignored warnings after visiting an Iranian port, and attacks on tankers near Oman have continued since the U.S. election.

Others see the same risk. Rapidan Energy, an energy consulting firm, puts the chance that fighting resumes at 80%. Its president, Bob McNally, expects crude to climb back above $100 a barrel if it does.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

The pattern since the spring is clear enough to watch. We matched every Brent trading day since March 2 with BTC’s move on the same date, 176 days in all.

Last week showed both sides. On Wednesday, Brent fell 8.7%, and BTC rose 3.9%. On Thursday, Brent rose 3.9%, while BTC fell 5.5%.

The link is loose, not fixed. Both prices react to the same war headlines, and on a third of the big oil-up days, BTC still rose. The timing is also approximate, because Brent settles in New York while Binance’s daily candle closes at midnight UTC.

Still, a renewed oil spike would hit BTC at a weak moment, with the price already below its long-term average.

On the daily chart, BTC is also below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that weight recent prices more. They sit at $76,492 for 200 days and $79,279 for 50 days.

For Bitcoin, the oil market is now a risk worth watching. If talks with Iran collapse and Brent jumps, the pattern since March points to more pressure on BTC.

#5335. Polygon Plans Hard Fork to Seize $6.5 Million From Polymarket and Binance Hackers

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Polygon developers now propose a step that has long been considered an absolute taboo in the crypto industry. They put to a vote a plan to rescue Binance and Polymarket money, and this plan is, to say it mildly, radical — zero out the hackers’ wallets at the protocol level. Ongoing cybersecurity crisis shows no signs of stopping, and now the industry is being faced with an uncomfortable choice: save systemic players or protect the inviolability of Web3’s main rule that transactions cannot be reversed. The Polygon PoS hard fork involves seizing 70.49 million POL tokens ($6.5 million at the time of the attack) from the hacker addresses to return them to the victims.

The crisis unfolded at the end of October after two independent hacks. The stolen assets were scattered across five wallets (23.86 million POL was taken from Polymarket, 46.63 million from Binance). Yes, Polygon validators immediately blacklisted the addresses, cutting off the outflow, but this is just an attempt to hold back the dam with bare hands. Manual blocking is a temporary plug, and the authors of the proposal openly admit it.

The hacker is not giving up either and is continuously bombarding the network with transactions carrying wild fees of up to 219,000 POL, counting on automation or a validator with a weakness for easy money to let the operation through for a windfall profit. Things have gone as far as direct attempts to bribe validators with cash, and the hacker simply ignored on-chain negotiations. The developers’ logic is simple: keeping millions in a manual “ban” forever is a dead end that leaves the entire network under constant fire.

No one has access to the hacker’s private keys, so Polygon is changing the consensus rules themselves. Should the hard fork get approval at a certain block, the hackers’ balances will be zeroed out, and an equivalent amount will be mirror-credited to verified Binance and Polymarket wallets — without any token printing.

Polygon Labs is well aware that such an administrative step completely negates the very idea of decentralization.

This plan inevitably triggers a strong sense of the notorious The DAO hard fork of 2016. Back then, to save the young Ethereum ecosystem, developers also had to go through a painful split of the community and ignore the “Code is Law” principle. But Polygon Labs hopes that in their case consensus among validators is already rock-solid, so they are narrowing the framework of the precedent as much as possible, positioning the fork as an exclusively one-time action.

The fate of the millions in POL token is being decided right now in a community vote. The largest validators are already in favor, since both platforms are critically important to Polygon’s survival. If the plan is approved, the software will be released after two weeks of testing, and exchanges and node operators will have to urgently update. Those who refuse to switch to the new code face automatic isolation on the old branch of the blockchain — with no connection to the main network.

For individuals who suspect their devices or wallet credentials may have been compromised, the reminder recommends creating a new wallet on a clean, updated device and transferring funds. Exposed seed phrases should never be reused.

Binance has resumed withdrawals in phases, with that of SHIB on the Ethereum network also enabled.

In a recent post, binance warns that opportunistic scammers may try to take advantage of this period as withdrawals resume in phases.

Scammers may impersonate Binance through DMs, emails, group chats and even small transfers with a message attached, offering to "speed up withdrawals," give "priority processing," help to "claim compensation," or move assets into a "Binance vault," with users urged to take precautions.

Users should remember that Binance will never contact them first about their account or funds, nor offer or sell them a place in the withdrawal queue or charge a fee to unlock a network or asset.

#5333. South Korea Announces Delay in Crypto Taxation Policy

South Korea announced a delay in the introduction of its cryptocurrency capital gains tax until 2029, extending the tax-free period by two years as authorities plan on strengthening regulatory oversight and connecting data from exchanges with the United States, yna.co.kr reports.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il announced the proposal Thursday, acknowledging that the government would be postponing the controversial tax for a fourth time already.

Originally, the policy was scheduled to become active in January 2022: it would impose a 22% tax, local income tax on all cryptocurrency-related gains that exceed 2.5 million won.

While the proposed delay could provide a relief for the South Korean cryptocurrency market and even support the domestic trading activity, it remains a substantial risk factor for both local and overseas investors.

Officials argue that implementing the tax before international information-sharing systems become operational could disadvantage local exchanges and complicate enforcement against overseas trading activity.

Future tax liabilities aren't going to be eliminated, additional time to develop a comprehensive taxation network is more likely to enforce even more limitations on investors in the future, rather than a premature implementation with various legal loopholes.

The government also intends to introduce provisions allowing investors to carry forward cryptocurrency investment losses for up to three years, potentially reducing taxable gains in subsequent periods.

South Korea is also going to establish a separate working group that is going to further refine taxation rules and hopefully simplify reporting requirements for investors, considering the complexity of reporting digital assets transactions and traders on exchanges.

Legislative amendments are expected to reach the National Assembly in 2027.

Authorities reported the continuous coordinating with the Financial Services Commission to accelerate digital assets legislation, providing more transparency and investors protection.

For the industry in general, the proposed extension is more of a transition stage that should improve the competitiveness of the digital assets market, despite introducing stricter tax enforcement. Unfortunately for retail investors, it creates another barrier that might push fresh funds further away from the industry.

#5331. Coinbase Bank Gets Full OCC Approval as Ripple Leads Crypto Banking Push

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Coinbase has moved closer to the center of the US financial system after securing full approval for its national trust bank charter. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) recorded the charter as effective on November 6. The development gives Coinbase a federally supervised framework for expanding its institutional custody and digital asset services.

The approval completes a process that began with Coinbase’s application in October 2025. The OCC granted conditional approval on April 2, 2026, before recording the charter as consummated. Coinbase can now operate through its national trust company under federal supervision.

Coinbase follows Ripple’s final OCC approval on October 26. Two major crypto companies have now secured national trust bank charters within weeks. Their progress shows how digital asset firms are increasingly seeking access to regulated financial infrastructure rather than operating outside traditional banking frameworks.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Coinbase’s approval follows a similar regulatory path taken by Ripple. The company received conditional approval for Ripple National Trust Bank in December 2025. Its final approval arrived on October 26, completing the process ahead of Coinbase.

Ripple’s charter has specific implications for its stablecoin business. Ripple National Trust Bank can manage the segregated reserves backing RLUSD. It can also act as collateral trustee and provide fiduciary digital asset custody services.

RLUSD will continue to be issued by Standard Custody & Trust Company, Ripple’s New York-regulated trust company. The new federal charter adds another layer of supervision around its reserve management and institutional services.

Coinbase Bank has a different commercial opportunity. Its national trust company can provide federally supervised custody and fiduciary services to institutional clients. Coinbase previously said the charter would support its Prime custody business and other regulated services.

The growing number of crypto trust bank approvals has not gone unchallenged. The Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) filed a lawsuit against the OCC on October 2. The group argues that the regulator exceeded its authority by expanding access to national trust charters.

The banking association claims crypto companies receive federal banking credibility without meeting several requirements imposed on traditional banks. These include FDIC insurance, certain capital and liquidity standards, and Community Reinvestment Act obligations.

🚨 BIG: ICBA Sues OCC Over Crypto Trust Bank ChartersThe Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) has sued the OCC, arguing that its rules allowing crypto firms to obtain national trust bank charters exceed the agency’s legal authority and do not impose the same… pic.twitter.com/kJ8fVcXPoj

The lawsuit challenges the OCC’s March 2026 rule and related guidance. It argues that the regulator has stretched the national trust charter beyond its original statutory purpose.

The dispute could have consequences beyond Coinbase and Ripple. A successful challenge could complicate the regulatory pathway for other digital asset companies pursuing similar charters.

However, the OCC’s approach reflects a wider shift in US financial regulation. The agency has increasingly opened the door to crypto custody, payments, and stablecoin-related activities under federal supervision. This shift also creates opportunities for emerging blockchain infrastructure projects.

Coinbase Bank’s approval represents more than another regulatory milestone. It shows that crypto companies are competing for a larger role in the financial infrastructure institutions will use.

Bitcoin is about to enter its ‘third phase’ of global adoption, according to Adam Back, the CEO of Blockstream. In an interview this week (as tracked by Wu Blockchain), the legendary British cryptographer said BTC is preparing to enter this new growth phase. He termed it the ‘third phase’ of international adoption.

As per the CEO’s revelation, Bitcoin is entering a new phase of adoption. The executive indicated that the asset has had two stages of adoption. The first phase ran from 2011 to 2019. During this period, the decentralized currency attracted individuals to buy it and miners to mine it. During this time, BTC’s price surpassed $1 and later reached hundreds of dollars.

The second phase has been an institutional era from 2020 to the present. Institutional interest increased massively during this period, and BTC surged to a record $69,000 in November 2021, then climbed above $100,000 in August 2025. Institutional participation grew as ETFs validated Bitcoin’s legitimacy and made it easier for traditional investors to access.

In the podcast, Back said that the flagship cryptocurrency is on the verge of entering its ‘third wave’ of global adoption. According to the CEO, this period is unique and different from other phases. In this evolving era, traditional banks and other recognized investment institutions are preparing to further drive global Bitcoin adoption, the executive said.

As Back noted, the ‘third phase’ of institutional Bitcoin adoption is primed to be fueled by major investment banks and professional asset management channels, whose participation has yet to fully materialize.

The CEO revealed that some major investment banks have recommended a 2%-4% Bitcoin allocation in their model portfolios. #5329. Binance Revokes API Keys, Security Issue Found at SignalPlus

Binance has revoked all API keys associated with SignalPlus after the digital asset trading infrastructure provider identified a potential security vulnerability, prompting the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange to take measures to protect users, according to the latest report on the Binance's official Square feed.

The exchange confirmed Thursday that the decision was intended to prevent possible unauthorized access through connections established between Binance accounts and SignalPlus. Binance emphasized that its internal systems had not been compromised and that customer funds remained safe.

For now, the reason or the nature of the incident remains unclear. Both companies have yet to disclose how serious the potential vulnerability is or how many users may be affected. The development underscores the security challenges associated with third-party infrastructure in cryptocurrency markets, where trading platforms increasingly depend on external applications for execution, analytics and automation.

Binance's security documentation advises users to revoke potentially compromised credentials immediately and restrict API permissions to necessary functions.

For affected SignalPlus users, restoring automated trading functionality may require generating new credentials once the integration is deemed secure.

SignalPlus provides trading infrastructure and analytical tools for cryptocurrency derivatives markets, allowing traders to manage positions and execute strategies across exchanges through API integrations.

These connections enable third-party applications to interact with exchange accounts without requiring users to transfer their assets off-platform. However, depending on the permissions granted, compromised API credentials can potentially expose accounts to unauthorized trading activity.

Binance has effectively severed existing integrations between its platform and SignalPlus. The measure could potentially disrupt automated trading strategies that rely on those connections.

#5328. Strategy Buys $82M in Bitcoin as STRC Tokenized Stock Adds New Twist to Saylor’s BTC

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Strategy Bitcoin holdings climbed to 850,364 BTC after Michael Saylor’s company purchased another 1,036 Bitcoin for $81.9 million. The latest acquisition came as Bitcoin traded below the company’s average purchase price, putting its enormous treasury under renewed market pressure.

According to a November 9 SEC filing, Strategy bought the Bitcoin between November 2 and 8 at an average price of $79,012 per coin. Its total acquisition cost now stands at $64.16 billion, with an average purchase price of $75,456.

Strategy has acquired 1,036 $BTC and repurchased $188M of $STRC. As of 11/8/26, we hold 850,364 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets. $MSTR https://t.co/Pxqso5aVRU

The latest purchase also coincided with a $188.3 million repurchase of Strategy’s STRC preferred shares. The company funded both transactions through its common-stock offering program, highlighting how Michael Saylor continues using capital markets to finance its Bitcoin accumulation.

Strategy sold 2,051,348 shares of its Class A common stock through its at-the-market offering program during the reporting period. The sales generated $283.8 million in net proceeds. The company allocated then $81.9 million toward Bitcoin purchases, while $188.3 million went toward repurchasing 1,887,464 STRC preferred shares. Another $13.6 million was allocated to its general USD cash balance.

The latest transactions show how Strategy accumulation involves more than simply issuing shares and purchasing Bitcoin. The company is also actively managing its preferred securities and liquidity.

Strategy maintained approximately $4.77 billion in its USD Reserve and another $146.2 million in general USD Cash. This reserve supports preferred-stock dividends and interest payments on outstanding debt.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin’s decline below Strategy’s average acquisition price has put its treasury underwater on paper. At $74,000 per BTC, the company’s holdings would carry an unrealized loss exceeding $1 billion. But the latest purchase shows that Saylor has not backed away from accumulation despite the weaker market environment.

The $188.3 million repurchase also puts Strategy’s preferred securities back into the spotlight. STRC, known as Stretch, is a variable-rate perpetual preferred stock designed to trade around its $100 stated amount. It pays cash dividends, with its rate adjusted periodically to encourage price stability.

The instrument has also entered the tokenized securities market through Ondo Finance’s STRCon. Launched in April 2026, STRCon provides blockchain-based economic exposure to Strategy’s Stretch preferred stock. The token is available across Ethereum, Solana, and BNB Chain, subject to geographic and investor restrictions.

Tokenholders receive economic exposure and dividend-related benefits, but do not obtain conventional shareholder voting rights. This gives Strategy’s digital credit securities another distribution channel. Investors outside traditional brokerage platforms can access tokenized exposure through supported blockchain infrastructure.

However, tokenized trading does not generate fresh capital for Strategy automatically. Secondary-market transactions change ownership between investors and do not directly fund additional Bitcoin purchases. Still, this fits into Strategy’s longer-term ambition to build digital credit products for an increasingly tokenized financial system.

Strategy’s latest purchase arrived during a difficult period for institutional Bitcoin demand. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.3 billion in net outflows last week. Last Friday alone accounted for $411.9 million in withdrawals.

BlackRock’s IBIT led Friday’s outflows with approximately $403 million in redemptions. Fidelity’s FBTC recorded $42.8 million in inflows, offering only a partial offset.

Bitcoin also fell toward $74,000 this morning, reaching its weakest level since August. The decline followed broader crypto selling pressure and growing concerns surrounding regulatory uncertainty as AI stocks slide.

The contrast between ETF withdrawals and Strategy’s continued accumulation highlights two different approaches to Bitcoin exposure. ETF investors can reduce exposure through daily redemptions, while Strategy continues using equity financing and its preferred-stock structure to expand its treasury.

The latest Bitcoin acquisition from Strategy reinforces the company’s long-term commitment. Strategy Bitcoin holdings now exceed 850,000 BTC, leaving the company with more than 4% of Bitcoin’s maximum supply.

Whether that commitment pays off will depend heavily on Bitcoin’s next market cycle, alongside Strategy’s ability to maintain access to capital markets.

The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) has picked Avalanche as the only blockchain to settle tokenized stocks on its planned 24/7 trading platform, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens that track shares of real companies. The NYSE version would let investors trade U.S. stocks around the clock, settle trades instantly and pay with stablecoins, digital tokens that hold a steady $1 value.

The New York Stock Exchange has selected Avalanche ($AVAX) as the exclusive blockchain for settling tokenized U.S. stocks on its upcoming 24/7 trading platform, according to the WSJ.NYSE cited Avalanche’s speed, throughput and compliance capabilities.The platform is targeting… pic.twitter.com/uE4S3X5lnn

AVAX jumped on the news. It rose 4.3% in the minute the reports hit at 12:30 UTC, and it trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% on the day while Bitcoin and Ether are down.

The pick lands on a chain that holds only a small slice of the market today. Avalanche carries $179 million of the $3.73 billion in tokenized shares tracked by rwa.xyz. That is 4.8% of the market, down from 10.3% a month ago.

So can the NYSE deal make Avalanche the main home for these tokens?

The plan is not new, but the blockchain is. NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) first announced the platform in January and said it would seek regulatory approval.

The tokens would not be copies. ICE said they would be interchangeable with ordinary shares and carry the same dividend and voting rights.

NYSE picked Avalanche for its speed, the number of trades it can handle, and its tools for meeting regulatory rules, the Journal reported. The platform is aiming for a fourth-quarter launch, but it still needs regulators’ approval.

ICE has also signed up Securitize to issue tokenized shares for companies and funds, under a deal announced this year.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

The NYSE deal would be a big step up. We pulled the latest network breakdown from rwa.xyz, which tracks tokenized shares that investors can hold in their own wallets.

The market itself is still small next to the stock market. All the tokens it tracks add up to $3.73 billion, held by about 4.8 million wallet addresses.

The NYSE could change that scale. Every share settled through its platform would move on Avalanche, which no other chain can claim today.

There is a catch. Companies can refuse to have their shares tokenized. On OKXICE, a separate venue from OKX and ICE, 33 of the 62 companies first named had objected by late October.

Not yet. AVAX trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% from Monday’s opening price of $7.94, its best day since September 20.

The buying was heavy. In the hour that started at 12:00 UTC, about $11.8 million of AVAX changed hands on Binance. That is about 16 times a typical hour and the third-busiest hour in the past 1,000.

On the daily chart, AVAX is just below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that weight recent prices more. The 50-day and 200-day EMAs both sit at about $9.05, so one level now does the work of two.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

For tokenized stocks, the NYSE pick is the biggest vote yet for a single chain. For AVAX, the test is whether buyers can push it above $9.05 once the initial excitement fades.

According to one of the architects of the XRP Ledger, now Ripple CTO Emeritus David Schwartz, his retirement from active development almost a year ago came at the right time. "I picked a great time to retire!", said Schwartz, reacting to the latest report from OpenAI researchers, which touches on testing a new cyber model. Just one autonomous run and the AI completely changed the familiar standards of network security, OpenAI researcher Eric Wallace confirms.

The report shows how OpenAI's pipeline works. First thing to understand, it's a fully complete cycle: the system independently finds a potential bug, verifies it, writes a working exploit to confirm it and automatically releases a patch. This was tested on the Linux kernel, the core software that runs most of the planet's servers (including OpenAI's own compute clusters).

The Web3 sphere is one where open-source code is the foundation of blockchain security, so this development is a challenge to say the least. If AI finds zero-day vulnerabilities in a matter of hours, manual code auditing by humans becomes useless.

Yes, Schwartz stepped down from the post of Ripple CTO into honorary retirement last November, but he hasn't abandoned his terminal. Just recently he showed monitoring charts of his personal server hub on the XRP Ledger network. There, a node is running under colossal load: it maintains more than 550 active connections (peers), shows latency of around 200ms and processes about 110,000 incoming messages per second.

Besides, Schwartz continues personal work on the network's internal architectural problems. In a discussion with active validators, Schwartz detailed a transaction queue bug that caused the local load metric on his server to jump to 540, triggering fee spikes within the ledger.

Schwartz picked the "right time" to step back from Ripple, but he's clearly not out of the game.

#5322. Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.
